hotu-belt-8000: The dates from the 1950s excavations have large errors; the nearest reliable date is c. 10,700 years ago.
sang-e-chakhmaq-8000: Aceramic village; the earliest date (c. 9,900–9,550 years ago) falls just after the date of the map.
obishir-8000: Hunter-gatherers of the foothills in the south of the Fergana Valley: the Obishir 1 and Obishir 5 rockshelters; microliths, ornaments of stone and bone.
kurteke-8000: A rockshelter at almost 4,000 m — one of the highest Stone Age sites in Asia; a seasonal hunters' camp. The stone tools are of the same type as at Obishir V.
middle-ganga-8000: Hunter-fishers at the lakes of the Ganga plain: Damdama, Mahadaha, Sarai Nahar Rai; burials inside the camps. The bone dates of these sites are scattered and considered unreliable.
balangoda-8000: The nearest dates are about 11,800 and 8,700 years ago (Fa-Hien Lena); the culture is known from c. 38,000 to c. 3,000 years ago, but there are no direct dates for this time.
shangshan-8000: Early villages with pottery; rice is still wild or at an early stage of domestication.
lijiagou-8000: Microblade hunters who already made pottery, and above them one of the first settled villages of Central China (grinding stones, much pottery).
nanzhuangtou-8000: Nanzhuangtou, Donghulin, Zhuannian — hunter-gatherer sites with early pottery and grinding stones; possibly the first experiments with millet. Nearby at Cishan are pits with millet of the same date (the dating is disputed).
zengpiyan-8000: Zengpiyan cave near Guilin: hunters, fishers and shellfish gatherers with early coarse pottery; occupied c. 12,000–7,000 years ago.
jomon-8000: Initial Jōmon: settled hunters, fishers and gatherers with pottery; the first shell middens.
hokkaido-8000: The Taisho 6 site dates from about 11,000 years ago, with no known break in occupation afterwards. Hokkaido was then joined to Sakhalin and the mainland.
hoabinhian-8000: A technocomplex rather than a single culture: forager groups of caves and river valleys sharing a tradition of pebble tools ("sumatraliths"). The plants they used were wild. The area roughly spans the sites dated close to this time: Con Moong (Vietnam), Tam Hang (Laos), Steep Cliff, Spirit Cave, Lang Kamnan, Moh Khiew (Thailand), Gua Gunung Runtuh (Malaysia), Laang Spean (Cambodia); between them there are no dated sites. In north-eastern Vietnam — the caves of the Bac Son culture (Lang Son, Thai Nguyen, Cao Bang, Bac Kan, Ha Giang, Tuyen Quang): pebble tools with ground edges, later coarse pottery. Vietnamese archaeologists regard it as a separate culture (12,000–5000 years ago), foreign ones as a late variant of the Hoabinhian. When the Hoabinhian ended in the lowlands of northern Vietnam is debated: about 9500 years ago according to foreign syntheses, about 8300–7000 according to Vietnamese ones. On the island of Nias off Sumatra — the cave of Tögi Ndrawa (layers from about 12,000 years ago, after H. Forestier).
niah-8000: Burials in the West Mouth of the cave (seated and flexed), c. 12,000–7,500 years ago. The seated burials on hearths are perhaps younger — about 8000 years ago; then the cave was left for almost 4000 years.
gunung-sewu-8000: Caves of the Gunung Sewu hills in southern Java: pre-Neolithic layers c. 12,000–4,000 years ago (Braholo, Song Keplek); Gua Mandung and Seropan caves lie in the same karst.
palawan-8000: Ille, Pasimbahan-Magsanib, Tabon; Ille has one of the oldest cremations in Asia (c. 9,500–9,000 years ago).
mindoro-8000: According to the excavators, Bubog 1 was occupied without a break from the Pleistocene until c. 4,000 years ago; there are no dates within ±1,000 years of this map.
gebe-8000: The only date of this time at Golo Cave is considered doubtful by the excavators; the nearest reliable ones are about 11,700 and 7,900 years ago.
laili-8000: Hatu Saur rockshelter near Laleia village: the first phase of occupation c. 10,700–9,000 years ago; in nearby Laili Cave the layers run from about 44,000 to 11,000 years ago. In the east of the island — Matja Kuru 2 cave by Lake Ira Lalaro (c. 13,100–8200 years ago).
xianrendong: Xianrendong cave has some of the oldest pottery in the world (c. 20,000 years ago); hunters and gatherers, including of wild rice.
azilian-rhone: The Azilian of the Rhône valley and the Northern Alps: the burial cave of Aven des Iboussières (c. 10,000 BC, Azilian tools), Le Romain, La Fru, Jean-Pierre I, the caves of the Vercors; in the south, the Cornille rockshelter and the late Azilian of the Luberon.
direkli: A seasonal camp of wild goat (bezoar) hunters; geometric microliths, round structures, burials. By the excavators' summaries the cave dates from c. 12,000 to 9000 BC; dates of individual layers are not published.
sahout: Sites beneath life-size engravings of camels, ibex, wild asses and aurochs. Dates c. 12,800–11,400 years ago (OSL with errors of 1,000–2,000 years and one radiocarbon date of c. 11,400). Points like those of the early Levantine Neolithic (PPNA). The first inhabitants of inner Arabia after the Last Glacial Maximum; the engravings marked seasonal lakes and the routes between them.
gruta-del-indio: Gruta del Indio (Rincón del Atuel): hearths above a layer of ground-sloth dung, c. 12,400–11,300 cal BP; no fishtail points here.
sahout-8000: Hunters of the Sahout region in the PPNB (c. 10,300–8,700 years ago): points and cores as in the Levant, grinding stones; they still carved life-size camels on the rocks.
pampas-early-holocene: Hunter-gatherers of the Pampas in the early Holocene. Laguna de los Pampas (Lincoln): burial of an adult and a child, direct dates on teeth of 8971 ± 77 and 8835 ± 83 radiocarbon years (c. 10,240–9,590 cal BP). Caves and rockshelters of Tandilia — Cueva Zoro, Alero El Mirador, El Alfarache (c. 10,200–9,550 cal BP); El Guanaco 2 — early Holocene burials. Arroyo Seco 2 — camps from c. 9,500 cal BP, burials from c. 8,550.
southern-new-england: The Early Archaic of southern New England: quartz tools with very few bifaces — not Palmer and Kirk; perhaps a southern variant of the Gulf of Maine tradition. Sandy Hill (Mashantucket, Connecticut) — semi-subterranean houses, c. 10,200–9,400 cal BP; Route 169 East, Charlestown Meadows, Edgewoods.
kudlaevka: Kudlaevka culture: the Early Mesolithic of Lithuania, Belarus and Ukrainian Polesia; some authors derive it from the Swiderian. Liuban 9 (Belarus) — by radiocarbon, the end of the 10th to the beginning of the 8th millennium BC; Pabartoniai 1 (Lithuania) — AMS c. 10,200–9,800 cal BP; 18 settlements in Lithuania (mid-Preboreal to the first half of the Boreal), about 70 sites in Belarus. In Ukraine it is dated only by typology: at the map date the culture is just beginning (archaic sites of the Krynytsia and Brody types, Martynovychi I).
foothill-mountain: Two areas. The 'Foothill–Mountain' late Paleoindians (Alder, Hardinger and Lovell complexes; c. 9400–7800 radiocarbon years): hunters of bighorn sheep, deer and small game in the basins and mountain valleys — not bison hunters of the steppe like the Plano. The Wyoming Basin: Helen Lookingbill, Split Rock, McKean–Ryka (continuous occupation); south-western Montana: Barton Gulch (Ruby valley). In the south, in Idaho, — Veratic Rockshelter in the Birch Creek valley (8850 ± 40 radiocarbon years).
claussen: The lower cultural layers date to c. 10,500–10,250 cal BP, the upper 'Paleoarchaic' hearth to c. 10,200–9,500. There are no diagnostic tools in the layer; Dalton points were found downstream. An 'Archaic' economy (deer, turkey, mussels) — closer to the eastern woodlands than to the bison hunters of the Plains.
atuel-early-holocene: Hunter-gatherers of the Atuel valley in the early Holocene: Gruta del Indio (Rincón del Atuel) — hearths c. 10,500–8,000 cal BP; Arroyo Malo 3 in the mountains (c. 2,500 m) — from c. 10,000 cal BP; El Mallín (upper Atuel) — c. 10,000 cal BP.
capsian-6000: Upper Capsian (c. 6400–5400 BC): hunter-gatherers with geometric microliths (trapezes, triangles), pressure-flaked bladelets and shell middens (escargotières); in the west (Medjez II near Sétif, Aïn Naga) — from earlier levels. They held the whole Capsian range — from the High Tell (Jebba) and the Gulf of Hammamet (Hergla) to Ouled Djellal and the Ouled Naïl mountains (Rabah, Aïn Naga); in the south-east — to Medenine (an ostrich-eggshell date of c. 6000 BC, attribution unpublished). Around 6000 BC they begin to make pottery — at Hergla, Kef Hamda and Aïn Naga — but have no livestock yet: it arrives c. 5450 BC (Doukanet el Khoutifa).
west-maghreb-6000: Three areas. Eastern Rif (Morocco): Ifri Oudadane and Ifri Ouzabour caves, occupied c. 11.0–5.7 thousand cal years ago by Epipalaeolithic hunter-gatherers; pottery and farming arrive here c. 5650 BC. Middle Atlas: Ifri Ouberrid cave near Azrou — Epipalaeolithic hunters until c. 5600 BC. Western Algeria: the Columnatian (Columnata, Saint-Trivier); around 5750 BC the Upper Capsian reaches it (Columnata, Vigne Delosh I near Tiaret). The outline is common to the three areas with finds; no sites of this date have been found between them.
eastern-sahara-6000: Hunter-gatherers and the first herders of the Western (Libyan) Desert: Nabta — Kiseiba, Dakhla (Bashendi A), Kharga (Kharga B), Djara A/B, Farafra (Wadi el-Obeiyid), Abu Minqar, Selima, the Gilf Kebir, Regenfeld. A common 'bifacial' tradition: arrowheads with flat retouch, grinding stones, round huts on stone slabs; pottery in the 'Khartoum' style — from the mid-7th millennium BC; goat and sheep bones at Farafra — about 6000 BC. Around 6000 BC there was a short decline in settlement (a drought).
ounjougou-6000: Bandiagara plateau (Mali): some of the oldest pottery in Africa — phase 1 c. 9400–8400 BC, phase 2 c. 8100–6700 BC (Ravin du Hibou, Damatoumbou: quartz microliths, comb-decorated pottery, grinding stones); the next dates at Ravin du Hibou are c. 5600 BC.
eburran-6000: The Eburran industry at the boundary of phases 3 and 4 (c. 8,500–8,000 and c. 7,800–6,600 years ago; the type site of both is Gamble's Cave II): hunter-gatherers of the Nakuru, Elmenteita and Naivasha basins. Enkapune ya Muto cave on the Mau escarpment is occupied from c. 5300 BC.
hora-6000: The Hora 1 rockshelter (northern Malawi) was used c. 21,000–8,000 years ago; the Hora 2 burial is dated to 8170–7960 cal BP.
wilton-6000: Hunter-gatherers of southern Africa at the turn from the Oakhurst to the Wilton. The microlithic Wilton industry (segments, small scrapers, ostrich eggshell beads; c. 8,000–4,000 years ago) is already present by 6000 BC in the south and east (Melkhoutboom, Matjes River, Nelson Bay, Wonderwerk, Rose Cottage); in the Lesotho highlands and in the north the non-microlithic Oakhurst with large 'Woodlot' scrapers still lives on (Sehonghong, Liphofung, Kruger Cave). The dry interior — the Karoo and Namaqualand — is thinly settled at this time.
matobo-6000: Matobo Hills (Zimbabwe): after the Pomongwan industry (of the same family as the Oakhurst) — a microlithic tradition of Wilton type (Nswatugi and Pomongwe caves).
chessungalane-6000: Open-air site on the Save river. Horizon III (c. 8,600–6,700 years ago, OSL) — the transition from Oakhurst to Wilton; dates are from the sediment.
paleo-arctic-6000: Late Denali complex — hunters with microblades and wedge-shaped cores (American Paleo-Arctic tradition) in interior Alaska, the Brooks Range, the upper Susitna and south-west Yukon. Sites dated to this time: Onion Portage, Dry Creek, Broken Mammoth, Panguingue Creek, Owl Ridge, Teklanika West; in the Brooks Range — Tingmiukpuk and Gallagher; on the upper Susitna — Jay Creek Ridge. In south-west Yukon (Canyon, Annie Lake) — the Little Arm phase with microblades; the oldest dates there are about 8000 years old. Later, from about 6000 radiocarbon years ago, the Northern Archaic with side-notched points.
great-basin-archaic-6000: Early Archaic of the Great Basin: hunters and gatherers with side-notched points and grinding stones, after the stemmed-point tradition (also called the Western Pluvial Lakes Tradition). Sites dated to this time: Hogup and Danger caves (Utah), Bonneville Estates (Nevada), Fort Rock and Dirty Shame (Oregon); on the shores of former Lake Lahontan — Leonard Rockshelter and Fishbone Cave with basketry about 8000 years old. About 7700 years ago the region was covered by ash from the eruption of Mount Mazama.
la-jolla-6000: La Jolla complex: foragers of the coast of southern California and northern Baja California — cobble tools, grinding stones, shell middens by lagoons (c. 9,000–3,000 years ago). Sites dated to this time — Del Mar, Red Beach, the Allan O. Kelly site.
archaic-east-6000: Hunters and nut gatherers of the eastern woodlands at the transition from the Early to the Middle Archaic: serrated Kirk Stemmed points, then Stanly; the bifurcate tradition (LeCroy, St. Albans) is slightly earlier. Sites dated to this time — Engelbert, Sheep Rock Shelter, Mifflinville Bridge (Pennsylvania), Muddy Brook Rockshelter (New York).
southern-new-england-6000: Middle Archaic of southern New England: Neville and Stark points, quartz tools. The Neville type site lies at Amoskeag Falls on the Merrimack (New Hampshire). Sites dated to this time: Annasnappet Pond, Seekonk 2 (Massachusetts); Sandy Hill (Connecticut) — the latest date about 8000 years ago.
kurils-6000: Around 6000 BC hunters and fishers from Hokkaido come to Iturup: pottery with comb-scraped and cord-impressed decoration, as in the Early Jōmon (Urahoro type), stone adzes and bifacial points (Yankito 1 and 2, c. 7900 years ago). Nearby, at Kitovyi, there are traces of an earlier Neolithic.
lindosa-6000: Serranía de La Lindosa (Colombian Amazon): by the date model of Morcote-Ríos et al., occupation phase 2 lasts 9500–5900 cal BP. Known for its rock paintings.
puna-junin-6000: Vicuña and guanaco hunters of the Junín and Huánuco puna: Panaulauca (phase 2b, until c. 5080 BC in radiocarbon years), Pachamachay (33 layers without a break), Telarmachay, Lauricocha II.
acha-6000: Early Archaic fishers and gatherers of the Arica coast: Acha 2, Quiani 9, Caleta Vitor 1; nearby in southern Peru — Quebrada de los Burros. Forerunners of the Chinchorro fishers.
piuquenes-6000: Alero Los Piuquenes, Río Blanco valley (upper Aconcagua), Chile: 12 dates from 10,115 ± 80 to 5915 ± 185 radiocarbon years (c. 11,700–6,700 cal BP).
patagonia-6000: Guanaco hunters of the Patagonian steppe and foothills of Santa Cruz and Aysén. Sites dated to this time — Baño Nuevo, Alero Cárdenas, Los Toldos, Cueva Maripe, Cerro Casa de Piedra 7; Cueva de las Manos has the famous hand paintings. About 7,700 years ago — a large eruption of the Hudson volcano. To the east, in the Deseado Massif, — Gruta Molina (lower layers ≈ 9200–7600 cal years ago). In the south-west, by Lake San Martín, — Cueva del Paisano Desconocido (6930 ± 40 radiocarbon years).
umbu-6000: Umbu tradition of southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paraná, São Paulo): hunter-gatherers with stemmed bifacial points. Garivaldino — 7250 and 6760 radiocarbon years; the tradition lasts until the 14th century AD. In the upper Uruguay valley — sites of the Humaitá tradition (Itapiranga). José Vieira (Ivaí river, Paraná; 6683 ± 355 radiocarbon years) — a site with large bifaces and no points; it used to be set apart as the "Humaitá tradition".
pampas-6000: Hunter-gatherers of the Pampas. Arroyo Seco 2 — a peak of burials c. 8400–7800 cal BP; Laguna de los Pampas (Lincoln) — Early Holocene burials and Middle Holocene layers; La Moderna; caves and rockshelters of Tandilia. La Tigra, Arroyo Chocorí; on the southern coast — Monte Hermoso 1 and La Olla (human footprints in coastal mud).
iron-gates-6000: Lepenski Vir culture — the Mesolithic of the Iron Gates gorge on the Danube: riverside settlements of Lepenski Vir, Vlasac, Padina, Hajdučka Vodenica, Icoana, Schela Cladovei; trapezoid houses, stone sculptures, burials. Around 6200–5900 BC the transition to the Neolithic begins here (contacts with the Starčevo culture).
finnmark-6000: Late Mesolithic of northern Norway: descendants of the first settlers (the Komsa culture); sea-mammal hunters and fishers from Harstad and Tromsø to the Varangerfjord, inland — the Kautokeino plateau. Sites dated to this time — Tønsnes and Skarpenes (Tromsø), Almenningen (Målselv), Solli (Tjeldsund), Slettnes (Sørøya), Cudejoganjalbmi (Kautokeino).
west-scandinavia-6000: Late Mesolithic of Norway and western Sweden: in Norway from c. 6300 BC — the Nøstvet culture (ground axes), in Sweden — the Lihult culture. Sites dated to this time — Brunstad, Skakkestad, Dørdal, Vistehulen (Norway), Gunnarsröd, Ödsmål (Bohuslän).
suomusjarvi-6000: Suomusjärvi culture: hunters and fishers of almost all of Finland — from the south coast (Vantaa, Satakunta) to Karelia, Kainuu and Lapland (Kuusamo, Kemijärvi, Inari, Enontekiö) — with quartz tools and slate adzes, close to the Kunda culture. Later, c. 5100 BC, it is followed by the Comb Ceramic culture.
kongemose-6000: Kongemose (c. 6400–5400 BC), the successor of the Maglemosian: hunters, fishers and gatherers of Denmark, Scania and northern Germany; settlements by the sea and fjords (Kongemose, Vedbæk, Ringsjöholm and Rönneholm in Scania, Jäckelberg-Huk off Poel). In the Netherlands north of the Vecht — the "Northwest Group" of the same tradition (De Leijen, Borger, Havelte); in the south-east — as far as Berlin (Schmöckwitz). By this time Doggerland was almost entirely under water.
britain-6000: Late Mesolithic of Britain: narrow geometric microliths (from c. 8,400 years ago). By this time Britain was already, or almost, an island. Sites dated to this time — from Cornwall and Gower to Scotland: Howick, Morton, Balneaves, Bolsay (Islay), West Runton, Inverness, An Corran (Skye), Ulva. In western Scotland — the "Obanian" shell middens (Druimvargie near Oban, Oronsay): most authors see them as camps of the same people for processing shellfish and fish, not as a separate culture.
komornica-6000: Komornica culture: the Mesolithic of western and central Poland (Całowanie, Komornica). The map date is its end: in eastern Poland the Janisławice culture with trapezes is already there, and in Pomerania the Chojnice–Pieńki culture takes shape at the end of the 7th millennium BC. Sites dated to this time — Dęby 29, Brześć Kujawski 3, Pomorsko 1, Krzekotówek.
central-france-6000: The "second" Mesolithic with trapezes in western and central France: from the Loire and Burgundy south to Auvergne, Cantal, Velay, Rouergue and Quercy, west to the Charente and the mouth of the Gironde. No regional groups are defined yet. Sites dated to this time — Cuze de Neussargues and Les Baraquettes (Cantal), Béraud and Longetraye (Velay), Roquemissou (Aveyron), Lascaux, Pergourie, Geay, Lède du Gurp, Bavans rockshelter (Doubs).
tardenoisian-6000: Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt (RMS) and Tardenoisian — the "second" Mesolithic with trapezes and Montbani blades: in the Netherlands south of the Vecht, in Belgium and Luxembourg — the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt group, in northern France — the Tardenoisian culture. Sites dated to this time — Zwolle, Urk, Swifterbant, Kampen-Reevediep, Hoge Vaart (Netherlands), Verrebroek, Meerberg II (Belgium), Echternach, Loschbour (Luxembourg), Le Rougemont (Eure).
late-meso-s-germany-6000: Late Mesolithic with trapezes (the "second" Mesolithic) in southern Germany, Alsace and Switzerland up to the Swiss Plateau. Sites dated to this time — Fohlenhaus and Ehingen-Mühlen (Swabian Jura), Mannlefelsen (Alsace), Birsmatten-Basisgrotte, Wauwilermoos, Zürich, Lausanne, Château-d'Oex (Switzerland).
late-meso-bohemia-6000: Late Mesolithic of northern Bohemia (Bohemian Switzerland): the Dolský Mlýn, Šídelník I and Bezděz rockshelters have dates of this time.
asturian-6000: Late Mesolithic of Cantabria and the Basque Country. On the coast of Asturias and Cantabria — the Asturian culture: shell middens with 'picks'. Sites dated to this time — Coberizas, Mazaculos II, La Garma B, Los Canes (burials).
muge-6000: Shell middens of the lower Tagus: Muge — Moita do Sebastião, Cabeço da Arruda, Cabeço da Amoreira — with hundreds of burials (c. 6500–5000 BC); nearby — Cova da Onça, Encosta de Sant'Ana (Lisbon), Buraca Grande.
nerja-6000: Mesolithic of Andalusia: Nerja Cave (Málaga), to the west along the coast — Bajondillo (Torremolinos; the last Mesolithic date is around 6100 BC), in the mountains — Los Castillejos (Montefrío) and Carigüela (Píñar). The Geometric Mesolithic is weakly expressed here.
kukrek-6000: Kukrek culture: the Crimean steppe (Kukrek, Vyshenne), the lower Dnieper and its rapids (Ihren 8: horizons of 8200–7600 BC and a late one after 6650 BC), up the Dnieper to Dereivka (a Mesolithic burial of 6360–5880 BC), the northern Azov coast (Kamyana Mohyla).
upper-kolyma-6000: Sumnagin culture in the Upper Kolyma: hunters of reindeer and elk at passes and river crossings — Buyunda III (c. 8600–8200 years ago), Zapyataya (c. 7800–7400 years ago), layer II of Siberdik. N. N. Dikov distinguished a separate Siberdik culture here; new excavations assign these sites to the Sumnagin tradition. On the Chersky Range, at Pridorozhnaya by Lake Momontai, stemmed points of the Uolba tradition have one date of about this time (c. 8000–7300 years ago, with a large error).
shigir-6000: Hunter-fishers of the eastern slope of the Middle Urals (Gorbunovo bog): the Late Mesolithic and, around this time, the Early Neolithic Koshkino culture.
konda-6000: Late Mesolithic of the taiga Konda basin: Leushi IX (c. 8,500–8,000 years ago) and other sites of the basin.
cis-baikal-6000: Early Neolithic of Cis-Baikal: hunters and fishers with net-impressed and cord-impressed (Khaita) pottery — Ust-Khaita and Gorely Les on the Belaya (layers c. 8400–6900 years ago); on the western shore of Lake Baikal — Sagan-Zaba II and Buguldeika (c. 8160–6900 years ago), hunters of the Baikal seal and hoofed animals; the same pottery in the Tunka valley (Elovka-Nugan I) and on the northern Angara (Ust-Yodarma II). In Irkutsk — burials of the Final Mesolithic Shchukino group. The large Kitoi cemeteries appear later, c. 7500 years ago.
sakhalin-6000: Around 6000 BC two traditions replace each other on Sakhalin: hunters with arrowheads on blades and thin-walled pottery close to the Initial Jōmon of Hokkaido (Slavnaya 5, Slavnaya 4, Puzi 2), and their successors with Soni and Chaivo pottery (Ado-Tymovo 4, Chaivo 6, Sadovniki 2). Obsidian was brought from Hokkaido.
khirokitia-6000: Khirokitia culture — the Aceramic Neolithic of Cyprus (c. 7000–5200 BC): round stone houses, the villages of Khirokitia and Kalavasos-Tenta; farming, goats, sheep, pigs, fallow deer. A village of the same culture stood at Cape Andreas (Kastros, the tip of the Karpas peninsula); the culture broke up in the first half of the 6th millennium BC (Legrand-Pineau 2009).
hacilar-6000: Late Neolithic of the Lake District (Turkey): Hacılar (levels IX–VI, c. 6500–6000 BC) and Kuruçay — clay figurines, fine pottery; Karain Cave near Antalya has a Neolithic assemblage of the same time. To the north-west, on the upper Meander, — Ekşi Höyük: houses with red lime-plastered floors, phase 4 c. 6200–6000 BC, phase 3 c. 6000–5875 BC (Dedeoğlu et al. 2023). To the east, on Lake Beyşehir, — Erbaba: its upper levels (c. 6400–6000 BC) are compared by pottery with Hacılar VI–IX; obsidian from Cappadocia (Dirican et al. 2026).
hotu-belt-6000: Caspian Neolithic on the southern Caspian plain: Neolithic layers with pottery in the Hotu and Belt (Kamarband) caves near Behshahr (the dates of the 1950s excavations have large errors) and open villages of the Neka plain — Touq Tappeh (≈ 6250–5800 BC) and Tepe Valiki (≈ 6600–5900 BC): a 2-metre layer, the same pottery as in the caves; more than 40 Neolithic sites are known on the plains (Abbasnejad Seresti et al. 2025).
sang-e-chakhmaq-6000: Sang-e Chakhmaq (Shahroud): the western mound is Aceramic Neolithic, the eastern mound is a ceramic Neolithic related to the Jeitun culture of southern Turkmenistan.
balangoda-6000: Balangoda culture of Sri Lanka: rainforest hunter-gatherers with microliths, known from c. 38,000 to c. 3,000 years ago (Fa-Hien-lena cave, Bellan-bandi Palassa). On map 6000* the zone also includes the south coast at the Bundala lagoons (Patirajawela, by OSL ≈ 7.6 thousand years ago).
peiligang-6000: Peiligang culture (Henan, c. 7000–5000 BC): settled farmers — millet, pigs, footed grinding slabs, cemeteries. Named after Peiligang near Xinzheng; Jiahu, with its bone flutes, is usually counted in the same circle. In the west, along the Yellow River, the culture reaches Bancun (Mianchi).
jomon-6000: Initial Jōmon: settled hunters, fishers and gatherers with pottery; shell middens, pit dwellings.
hokkaido-6000: Hokkaido: hunter-gatherer sites dated to this time — Higashimachi, Tomino 3, Kikonai; in the east of the island — groups of pit dwellings. La Pérouse Strait already separates the island from Sakhalin.
gebe-6000: Gebe island (Moluccas): Golo cave (8100–7641 cal BP) and Wetef (8327–8011) — hunter-gatherers who came by sea.
laili-6000: Hatu Saur rockshelter near Laleia village (Timor): the second phase of occupation — c. 8,800–6,300 years ago.
buka-6000: Ancestors of the Papuans. Kilu Cave on Buka: people lived here c. 29,000–20,000 years ago, returned c. 10,400–10,000 cal BP and stayed until c. 5400 cal BP; the layers contain charred canarium nuts (Wickler 2001).
tasmania-6000: Ancestors of the Tasmanian Aboriginal people (languages unknown). Tasmania has been an island since c. 11,000 years ago; the isolation will last until the 19th century. The culture is still close to that of the mainland; fish and bone tools were given up only c. 3,500 years ago. Sites: Parmerpar Meethaner and Warragarra (Mersey valley), Rocky Cape, Cave Bay Cave (Hunter Island), Palana dune (Flinders Island).
australia-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (languages unknown). The same core-and-scraper tradition as before; small backed tools spread later, c. 4,000–5,000 years ago. The areas are drawn from Early Holocene sites; in the Middle Holocene the number of sites grows. On the north-west coast — shell middens from the time the sea reached the present shore (c. 8000 years ago).
uninhabited-ice-6000: Remnants of the Laurentide ice sheet c. 8,000 years ago: the Labrador dome (Quebec–Labrador) and the ice north and west of Hudson Bay — Keewatin, Foxe Basin, the Melville Peninsula, southern Baffin Island (after the reconstruction of Dyke et al. 2003, slice c. 8,000 years ago). About 8,200 years ago the ice sheet broke up over Hudson Bay and Lake Agassiz drained into the sea.
anangula-6000: Anangula tradition — the earliest inhabitants of the Aleutian Islands, makers of blades struck from cores. The Anangula core and blade site is about 9000 years old; nearby is Anangula village; on Amaknak Island (Unalaska Bay) — Margaret Bay and Hog Island sites of the same tradition.
kodiak-6000: Early Ocean Bay I tradition: sea-mammal hunters of Kodiak Island. The oldest dated hearth on Kodiak is about 7860–7790 years old (Alagnaruartulik site on the Karluk River), 100–150 years after the map date; the first people may have come a little earlier.
old-cordilleran-6000: Old Cordilleran tradition (Cascade phase): leaf-shaped Cascade points, hunters and gatherers of the north-western forests and the Columbia Plateau. On the plateau the Cascade phase replaced the Windust phase about 9000 years ago; sites include Weis Rockshelter (Idaho), Kelly Forks and Five Mile Rapids near The Dalles on the Columbia. Sites of south-western Oregon — Stratton Creek on the Rogue River and Williams Creek — are placed here too. About 7700 years ago the region was covered by ash from the eruption of Mount Mazama (Crater Lake).
nw-coast-6000: Early sea hunters and fishers of the Northwest Coast. Sites dated to this time: Chuck Lake on Heceta Island — one of the oldest shell middens on the coast; Hidden Falls on Baranof Island; Ground Hog Bay on Icy Strait; Lawn Point and Arrow Creek on Haida Gwaii; the Dundas Islands near Prince Rupert (Far West Point); Namu on the central coast of British Columbia. No early sites are known yet on the mainland between the Dundas Islands and Namu — the ancient shoreline here may now be under water.
mojave-pinto-6000: Pinto complex — hunters and gatherers of the Mojave Desert: Pinto points (about 10,200–7500 years ago) and grinding stones. Sites dated to this time: Henwood (Fort Irwin) and Stahl (Little Lake, Owens Valley); the type finds come from the Pinto Basin.
buena-vista-6000: Buena Vista Lake (southern San Joaquin Valley): site Ker-116 on the south shore — a buried layer with stone crescents, a local variant of the San Dieguito complex. Dates on freshwater mussel shell, corrected for the reservoir effect, are about 8400–7700 years ago; uncorrected, the latest date ends just before the map date.
millingstone-6000: Millingstone Horizon (after Wallace, 1955): seed and shellfish gatherers of the California coast — handstones and milling slabs, cobble tools, shell middens. Local variants are Topanga (Los Angeles), Oak Grove (Santa Barbara) and La Jolla (San Diego). Sites dated to this time: Diablo Canyon, Glen Annie Canyon, Swordfish Cave, Malaga Cove, Christ College (Irvine); further north — Santa Cruz, Monterey, Coyote Creek (Santa Clara Valley), Los Vaqueros.
southern-channel-islands-6000: Southern Channel Islands (San Clemente, Santa Catalina, San Nicolas): early seafarers, sea-mammal hunters and fishers. Sites dated to this time: Eel Point (San Clemente) and Little Harbor (Santa Catalina).
eel-point-8000: San Clemente Island (southern Channel Islands): the Eel Point site — the oldest date is about 10,000 years old; seafarers, sea-mammal hunters and fishers.
channel-islands-6000: Northern Channel Islands of California (Santarosae, breaking up into today's islands as the sea rose): seafaring hunters and fishers of the Paleocoastal tradition. The Busted Balls shell midden on San Miguel Island is about 9500–8000 years old.
cape-region: Cape region (southern Baja California): the shores of La Paz Bay and Espíritu Santo Island, then joined to the peninsula. Paleocoastal foragers: fish, sea lion, turtles; hooks and ornaments of pearl-oyster shell. Covacha Babisuri cave was lived in from about 12,000 years ago to the 18th century; pearl oysters were worked here at least 8500 years ago.
cape-region-10000: Cape region (southern Baja California): Covacha Babisuri cave on Espíritu Santo Island (then part of the peninsula) — Paleocoastal shell gatherers and fishers. Settlement begins right at the map date: the oldest date of the cave is 11,930–11,230 years ago by one calibration and 12,370–11,870 by another.
borax-lake-6000: Borax Lake Pattern (after Fredrickson): hunters and gatherers of the North Coast Ranges of California — wide-stemmed points, milling stones. Clear Lake basin: Borax Lake, Mostin (burials) and Crazy Creek sites; here the Post Pattern gives way to the Borax Lake Pattern about the map date.
pilot-ridge-6000: North Coast Ranges of California: site CA-HUM-573 on Pilot Ridge (about 7900 years ago) — Borax Lake points, milling stones and the remains of a dwelling, the oldest structure in the region; sites of the same age in Del Norte County.
post-pattern-8000: Post Pattern (after Fredrickson) — the earliest culture of the North Coast of California (about 13,000–9000 years ago): large leaf-shaped and stemmed points, crescents by the lakes — a local variant of the stemmed-point tradition. Clear Lake basin: the burial and hearths of the Mostin site.
oshara-6000: Oshara tradition, Jay phase: hunters and gatherers of the Colorado Plateau and the San Juan Basin with long stemmed points. The Jay phase dates to about 7450–6750 radiocarbon years ago (about 6300–5600 BC). Sites dated to this time: Cowboy, Dust Devil and Old Man caves and Sudden Shelter (Utah), Arroyo Cuervo (New Mexico).
mountain-tradition-6000: Mountain Tradition (after Black, 1991): hunters and gatherers of the Southern Rocky Mountains — not Plains Archaic but descendants of Great Basin peoples; pit houses and high-altitude camps. Sites dated to this time: Middle Park (Hay Gulch), Lawn Lake, Swallow, Tenderfoot and Mountaineer (Gunnison), Hard Labor, Dutch John (Uinta Mountains).
plains-archaic-6000: Early Plains Archaic: bison hunters and gatherers with side-notched points, pit houses. The Mummy Cave complex — north-western plains and foothills (Mummy Cave, Head-Smashed-In, Oxbow Dam, Hawken, MacHaffie, Stud Horse Butte); the Logan Creek complex — the eastern edge of the prairies (Logan Creek, Cherokee Sewer, Simonsen, Itasca, Granite Falls, Swan River, Carver County sites in Minnesota). On the southern High Plains people were few (Cooper, Domebo, Blackwater Draw); the Llano Estacado and northern Texas seem to have been almost empty during the hot mid-Holocene. The northern edge lies at the Hardisty bison pound (Alberta) and Saskatoon.
texas-archaic-6000: Early Archaic of Central and South Texas and the eastern Trans-Pecos: Martindale, Uvalde and Bandy points, later the Calf Creek horizon. Sites dated to this time: Wilson-Leonard, Richard Beene, Fort Hood, Hall's Cave, Hinds Cave, Bonfire Shelter; in the Big Bend — Rendezvous and Burnt Draw.
wapekeka-6000: The oldest burials of north-western Ontario: human bone about 8000–7700 years old, almost exactly at the map date; the burials lie near the Wapekeka community.
gulf-of-maine-6000: Gulf of Maine Archaic tradition (after B. Robinson): quartz unifacial tools and ground stone, without Neville points. Sites dated to this time: Gilman Falls, Neal Garrison, Rumford Falls (Maine), Hormell (New Hampshire), Mud Lake Stream (New Brunswick). Coastal sites of that time are drowned by the rising sea.
belle-isle-6000: Early Maritime Archaic on the Strait of Belle Isle: the L'Anse Amour burial mound (about 8500–7800 years ago) — one of the oldest funerary monuments in North America; sites near Pinware, Blanc-Sablon and Saint-Augustin.
coahuila-6000: Coahuila complex: hunters and gatherers of the Cuatro Ciénegas basin. Frightful Cave (excavated by W. Taylor) was visited from about 7500 BC to about AD 185 by radiocarbon.
tamaulipas-6000: Archaic of the Tamaulipas sierras (after MacNeish, 1958): the Infiernillo phase in the Sierra Madre near Ocampo (Romero and Valenzuela caves, Infiernillo canyon) and the Lerma phase in the Sierra de Tamaulipas. The chronology is old and rests on a single radiocarbon date: about 7000–5000 radiocarbon years BC (about 7750–5850 BC).
oaxaca-6000: Hunters and gatherers of the Valley of Oaxaca: Guilá Naquitz and Cueva Blanca caves and the open camp of Gheo-Shih by the Mitla River (lower layer about 7600 BC). In Marcus and Flannery's scheme the Naquitz phase gives way to the Jícaras phase about 6000 BC; there are no direct dates for this time.
basin-mexico-6000: Southern lakes of the Basin of Mexico (Chalco and Xochimilco): Zohapilco (Tlapacoya) and San Gregorio Atlapulco — about 8000–7500 years ago, grinding stones with starch of maize, sweet potato and beans. They begin 50–150 years after the map date; earlier, Paleoindians lived here.
basin-mexico-10000: Paleoindians of the Basin of Mexico, on the shores of lakes Texcoco and Chalco: the Tlapacoya I skull is about 12,000 years old (AMS), the Peñón III woman about 12,700.
santa-marta-10000: Ocozocoautla caves (Chiapas): Santa Marta — occupied from about 12,500 years ago (13 charcoal dates); nearby Los Grifos — hunting of the Pleistocene horse.
santa-marta-8000: Ocozocoautla caves (Chiapas): in Santa Marta cave finds are few between about 9800 and 8500 years ago; the nearest dated layer is about 9700 years old.
santa-marta-6000: Santa Marta cave (Chiapas): layers about 8300 and 7600 years old; most finds date to around the cold event 8200 years ago.
peace-river-6000: The Peace River parkland — an island of grassland in the northern boreal forest. Charlie Lake Cave (British Columbia) was occupied from about 12,500 years ago; several dates fall around 8000 years ago, but with large errors (±290–350 years). A stratified site in a dune on top of Saskatoon Mountain near Grande Prairie (Alberta) has charcoal from about 8000 years ago. The tools from these levels are not published, so the people's culture is unknown.
cross-creek-8000: Early Millingstone of the central California coast: the Cross Creek shell midden with milling stones — about 10,300–9650 years ago (corrected for the marine reservoir); nearby — Diablo Canyon. Apart, by San Francisco Bay, — Los Vaqueros (Contra Costa): the first date 8810 ± 60 radiocarbon years, then a continuous occupation.
mojave-8000: Mojave Desert: the Lake Mojave complex — Lake Mojave and Silver Lake stemmed points along the shores of former Lake Mojave (Soda Lake, Silver Lake), about 13,800–9000 years ago. Dated sites: Henwood and Floodpond (Fort Irwin), Stahl (Little Lake).
el-riego-6000: The El Riego phase (Tehuacán Valley): hunters and gatherers who came together in larger groups in some seasons; the first known burials. AMS dates from Coxcatlán Cave: 9893–7838 cal BP. Before it — the Ajuereado phase. By the AMS dates from Coxcatlán the El Riego phase ends about 7840 years ago (about 5890 BC); then comes the Coxcatlán phase.
middle-cauca-8000: Sites of the Middle Cauca Valley (Caldas, Risaralda, Quindío: La Pochola, El Antojo, Salento, La Montañita and others): dates from ≈ 12,700 cal years ago (10,619 ± 66 radiocarbon years) through 10,255–10,160 and 9886–9537 cal years ago and on into the middle Holocene (Dikau et al. 2015; p3k14c database). Early foragers of the Andean forests. To the north, in Antioquia, — El Jazmín (dates from ≈ 11,700 to ≈ 6400 cal years ago). To the south-west, on the upper Calima, — Sauzalito (9670 ± 150 … 9300 ± 100 radiocarbon years) and El Recreo (8750 ± 160): hoe-axes with two notches for hafting, grinding stones, hammerstones, flakes; no projectile points (Salgado 1988–1990).
middle-cauca-6000: Preceramic foragers of the Cauca basin. The Middle Cauca (Caldas, Risaralda, Quindío: La Pochola, El Antojo, Salento, La Montañita and others): dates from ≈ 12,700 cal years ago into the middle Holocene (Dikau et al. 2015; p3k14c database); to the north, in Antioquia, — El Jazmín (dates until ≈ 6400 cal years ago). To the south-west — the Calima preceramic tradition (Salgado 1988–1990): El Pital, the first phase ≈ 7310 ± 140 radiocarbon years (≈ 8100 cal years ago), occupied until the 4th–3rd millennium BC. Common to both areas: hoe-axes with side notches for hafting, grinding stones and hammerstones of river pebbles, no projectile points; plant gathering (perhaps early gardens), small game hunting, fishing.
banwari-trace: Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad (by the Oropouche swamp) is the oldest known site in the West Indies: a shell midden of hunters, fishers and gatherers who came from the mainland. The lowest layer is ≈ 7900–7800 cal years old, slightly later than the map date; the next layers are ≈ 7400–6900 and 6200–5500 cal years old.
alaka: The Alaka phase: shell mounds of hunters, fishers and gatherers on the coast of northwestern Guyana, between the Pomeroon and Waini rivers. The oldest date is from Piraka (≈ 8050 cal years ago); Barambina ≈ 7700, Kabakaburi and Haimarakabra ≈ 6300 cal years ago; the mounds grew until ≈ 2500 radiocarbon years ago (Plew).
amotape-siches: The Amotape (≈ 11,200–8000 radiocarbon years ago) and Siches (≈ 8000–5000) phases of Richardson: hunters, fishers and gatherers of the far north coast of Peru (Piura — Talara), shell middens by mangrove lagoons. Sites: Siches, Amotape.
ayacucho-10000: Hunters and gatherers of the Ayacucho Basin (MacNeish excavations); in his scheme — the Jaywa phase. Jaywamachay cave: the earliest date is 10,280 ± 170 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,600–11,300 cal years ago) — the start of the sequence; the dates then continue without a break. The dates are old, with large errors.
ayacucho-8000: Hunters and gatherers of the Ayacucho Basin (MacNeish excavations); in his scheme — the Puente phase. Jaywamachay — 8980 ± 140 and 8645 ± 140 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,000 and 9650 cal years ago); Puente — 8860 ± 125 (≈ 9900). The dates are old, with large errors.
ayacucho-6000: Hunters and gatherers of the Ayacucho Basin (MacNeish excavations); in his scheme — the Piki phase. Puente — 7160 ± 125 radiocarbon years (≈ 8200–7700 cal years ago), Jaywamachay — 7105 ± 130 (≈ 8200–7650), Ayamachay — 7560 ± 125. The dates are old, with large errors.
chinchorro-6000: The Chinchorro culture: fishers and gatherers of the Atacama Desert coast (Acha 2, ≈ 9000 cal years ago, is the first Chinchorro settlement according to Arriaza). Sites of this time: Acha 2, Quiani 9, Caleta Vitor, Camarones 14 and 17; in southern Peru — Quebrada de los Burros and Ilo (Kilómetro 4, Ring Site, Villa del Mar); in the south — Tiliviche 1-B in a ravine 40 km from the sea (sea fish and shells: people moved between the coast and the ravines). Later, from ≈ 7000 years ago, the world's oldest artificial mummies appear here (Camarones).
morro-colorado: Fishers and gatherers of the Taltal coast (Archaic II, ≈ 8500–7500 years ago; Salazar et al. 2015), known from the lower layers of Morro Colorado. The points still follow the Huentelauquén tradition, but shell fish-hooks already appear — the beginning of the "shell fish-hook culture".
puna-jujuy-6000: Vicuña and guanaco hunters of the middle puna (Middle Archaic). Of this time — Hornillos 2 (layer 3; Susques); the earlier sites of the zone — Huachichocana, Inca Cueva, Pintoscayoc — are abandoned or in a gap by now.
antofagasta-8000: Archaic hunters of the Antofagasta de la Sierra puna (Catamarca): Quebrada Seca 3 — about 30 dates from ≈ 11,200 to ≈ 5600 cal years ago, including this time. To the north, at Pastos Grandes (Salta), — the Alero Cuevas rockshelter (from ≈ 9800 cal years ago).
antofagasta-6000: Archaic hunters of the Antofagasta de la Sierra puna (Catamarca), upper Las Pitas and Punilla rivers: Quebrada Seca 3 (7350 ± 80 … 7130 ± 110 radiocarbon years, ≈ 8100–7900 cal years ago), Cueva Salamanca 1, Peñas de la Cruz.
pichasca: Alero de Pichasca (San Pedro Viejo de Pichasca), Hurtado valley: a multi-layer rockshelter; dates of 9920 ± 110, 7050 ± 80 and 4700 ± 80 radiocarbon years (Ampuero & Rivera 1971). One date falls on this time: 7050 ± 80 (≈ 7980–7680 cal years ago).
central-chile-6000: Middle Archaic of central Chile (Archaic III of Cornejo and Saavedra, ≈ 8100–5600 cal years ago): Andean rockshelters — Los Piuquenes (upper Aconcagua) and El Manzano 3 (Maipo canyon; 8085–7640 cal years ago) — and the Cuchipuy cemetery by the former Tagua Tagua lagoon; nearby — the burial mounds of Santa Amelia de Almahue (5990–5720 BC). On the coast at Bucalemu — the Paso de las Conchas shell midden with a burial and a shell-bead workshop (7900–3780 BC). According to Henríquez and Gruzmacher, these were the same hunter-gatherers: seasonal camps in the valleys and on the coast, short stays in mountain rockshelters.
south-mendoza-6000: Hunter-gatherers of southern Mendoza. Gruta de El Manzano (Barrancas) — dates from ≈ 9050 to ≈ 7860 cal years ago; in the Atuel valley (Gruta del Indio, Arroyo Malo 3) the last dates are ≈ 8400–8000 cal years ago.
casa-de-piedra: Casa de Piedra 1 on the middle Colorado River (La Pampa, by today's reservoir): a hunter-gatherer site; dates of ≈ 9600, 8300 and 6900 cal years ago.
north-patagonia-6000: Hunter-gatherers of the Andean foothills of Neuquén: Epullán Grande in the Limay valley (≈ 7850 cal years ago), Cueva Haichol, Traful I; on the Chilean slope — Loconako 2.
fell-6000: Fell's Cave in the Pali Aike steppe (southern Patagonia): guanaco hunters; Early and Middle Holocene layers (dates of ≈ 8650 and ≈ 7830 cal years ago).
canoe-6000: Early maritime canoe hunter-gatherers of the channels of southern Patagonia. The oldest sites with bone harpoons are Ponsonby (eastern Riesco Island, Skyring Sound; ≈ 8400–7200 cal years ago) and Imiwaia 1 on the northern shore of the Beagle Channel; nearby — Túnel 7.
rincon-indios: Rincón de los Indios by Laguna Negra (eastern Uruguay): a hunter-gatherer site; one radiocarbon date of this time (≈ 8000 cal years ago).
cuareimense: The Cuareimense industry (after Hilbert, ≈ 8000–4500 radiocarbon years ago) on the left bank of the middle Uruguay River — from the Cuareim mouth to Salto Grande. Site W-52 — 7610 ± 245, 6420 ± 375 and 6300 ± 315 radiocarbon years; K-86 (Mandiyú) — 6760 ± 100.
nuagapua: Quebrada Ñuagapua (Bolivian Chaco, between Karaindaiti and Capirenda): the lower layer — from ≈ 8000 cal years ago (slightly before 6900 radiocarbon years) to ≈ 6000 radiocarbon years (Coltorti et al. 2010).
lower-amazon-6000: The Taperinha shell midden near Santarém has the oldest pottery of Amazonia (≈ 7800–7500 cal years ago); Pedra Pintada cave (Monte Alegre) has Paituna-phase pottery (≈ 7500–7000 radiocarbon years; Roosevelt 1995). They begin around the map date.
upper-madeira: Archaic of the upper Madeira: Teotônio at the rapids (Girau phase ≈ 9500–9400 cal years ago, Massangana phase ≈ 6500–6400 and ≈ 5700; Watling et al. 2018), Cachoeirinha 1 (≈ 9170, 7770 and 6920 cal years ago), Garbin (≈ 8490 and 6850).
abrigo-do-sol: Abrigo do Sol rockshelter (upper Guaporé, Mato Grosso): a continuous series of dates from ≈ 11,100 to ≈ 6500 cal years ago (Miller); of this time — 7220 ± 85, 7190 ± 70 and 7130 ± 85 radiocarbon years.
serranopolis: The Serranópolis phase (southwest Goiás, after Schmitz): after the Paranaíba phase of the Itaparica tradition, from ≈ 9000 radiocarbon years — simple flakes, more plants and molluscs in the diet. The GO-JA-01 rockshelter — about 30 dates from ≈ 12,500 to ≈ 7500 cal years ago, including this time.
central-minas-6000: Hunter-gatherers of central Minas Gerais — from the Lagoa Santa karst north to Montes Claros. Lagoa Santa: of this time — Lapa Vermelha IV and the Lagoa Santa site; some caves (Lapa do Santo) have a Middle Holocene gap (the "Archaic gap" of Araujo). The Chã do Caboclo rockshelter (≈ 150 km to the north): eight dates of 8400 ± 200 … 6630 ± 125 radiocarbon years, an unbroken series; of this time — 7300 ± 140 … 6820 ± 190 (≈ 8100–7650 cal years ago). The Lapa Pequena rockshelter (Montes Claros): seven dates of 8240 ± 160 … 7030 ± 100 radiocarbon years (the last ≈ 8000–7600 cal years ago), no later dates. At this time some caves of Central Brazil are already abandoned, others are still occupied.
jaguay-10000: Early maritime foragers of southern Peru. Quebrada Jaguay 280 (Arequipa coast, near Camaná) is one of the oldest fishing camps in the Americas (Jaguay phase; 11,105–9850 radiocarbon years, ≈ 13,000–11,200 cal years ago; Sandweiss et al. 1998): people caught small fish and gathered molluscs; obsidian was brought from the highlands (Alca, ≈ 130 km). Quebrada Tacahuay (near Ilo, ≈ 180 km to the south-east) — 13 dates of 10,770 … 9365 radiocarbon years (Keefer et al. 1998): butchering of seabirds (cormorants) and fish (anchovy).
jaguay-8000: Fishers and gatherers at Quebrada Jaguay (Arequipa coast): Machas-phase sites dated 8615 ± 135 and 8275 ± 130 radiocarbon years (≈ 9600 and 9200 cal years ago); the QJ-280 camp — until ≈ 8900 cal years ago.
el-jobo-10000: Hunters with El Jobo points (Falcón and Lara): Taima-Taima and Muaco — mastodon hunting at springs; Cucuruchú; the Río Pedregal basin (El Jobo); in the Lara Andes — El Vano (a ground-sloth kill). Reliable dates of El Jobo points are 17,800–12,600 cal years ago (Taima-Taima, Cucuruchú, El Vano); there are no direct dates for 10,000 BC.
furna-do-estrago: Furna do Estrago rockshelter (Brejo da Madre de Deus, Pernambuco): early layers ≈ 10,300–9500 cal years ago. The main cemetery of the shelter is much later, ≈ 2000 years ago.
north-coast-peru-6000: Preceramic farmers and fishers of the north coast of Peru (Dillehay ed. 2011). In the middle Zaña and Ñanchoc valleys (Andean foothills) — the Las Pircas (≈ 9800–7800 years ago) and Tierra Blanca (≈ 7800–5000 years ago) phases: round houses on stone foundations 200–400 m apart, storage pits; squash, peanut, beans, cotton, coca; irrigation ditches (from ≈ 7700 years ago); the Nanchoc mounds and cemetery. On the coast of the Chicama valley — the Huaca Prieta shell mound (occupied from ≈ 14,000 years ago) and Ascope 12. Sea fish from the coast is found at Ñanchoc too — the coast and the foothills were linked.
central-coast-peru-6000: Preceramic foragers of the central coast of Peru — from Ancón to Paracas. The village of La Paloma near Chilca (65 km south of Lima): the oldest layers are ≈ 7700 radiocarbon years old. People lived in round and oval semi-subterranean huts (floors dug 25–60 cm down, a frame of willow and cane, walls and roof of grass and reeds, mats on the floor; ≈ 11 m²) with a curved windbreak. The dead were wrapped in mats and buried in pits under the house floors. They ate mostly fish (≈ 70 %: anchovy, herring, drum, rock seabass), shellfish, sometimes sea lions, and plants of the lomas — the fog oases of the coastal desert; bottle gourds served as floats and containers, and obsidian was brought from Huancavelica (≈ 400 km). In the upper Chilca valley — the Tres Ventanas caves. The houses and burials of Paloma are known mostly from layers of ≈ 7000–5000 radiocarbon years ago. Sites dated to this time: Ancón, Chilca (village 304), La Paloma, Tablada de Lurín, Lino, Paracas (village 154), La Sentinela.
guitarrero-6000: Guitarrero Cave (Callejón de Huaylas): dates of 7730 ± 150 … 6610 ± 160 radiocarbon years (≈ 8500–7450 cal years ago); the dates are old, with large errors.
guitarrero-8000: Guitarrero Cave (Callejón de Huaylas): dates of 9140 ± 90, 8910 ± 90 and 8225 ± 90 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,300–9100 cal years ago).
carajas-6000: Hunter-gatherers of the caves of the Serra dos Carajás plateau (Pará, eastern Amazonia): N4WS-012 — 8240 … 6520 ± 70 radiocarbon years, Gruta do Gavião — 7925 ± 45 and 6905 ± 50 (≈ 7750 cal years ago).
carajas-8000: Hunter-gatherers of the caves of the Serra dos Carajás plateau (Pará, eastern Amazonia): Gruta do Pequiá — 9000 ± 50 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,200–9900 cal years ago) and later, NV-V — 8850 ± 40, CKS-30K — 8830 ± 40. These are the oldest dates of the area: the caves begin to be occupied about the map date.
las-vegas-6000: Fishers, hunters and gatherers of the Santa Elena Peninsula, Ecuador: site 80 (OGSE-80) and about 30 other sites. Early Las Vegas ≈ 10,000–8000 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,600–8800 cal years ago), Late Las Vegas ≈ 8000–6600 (≈ 9000–7300 cal years ago); a cemetery at site 80 and early cultivated plants (Stothert). Further east, on the Guayas coast, — El Muerto (7180 ± 80 radiocarbon years).
trombetas-boa-vista: The Boa Vista site (PA-OR-63) on the lower Trombetas (Pará): one date of this time — 7230 ± 50 radiocarbon years (≈ 8000 cal years ago); the next is ≈ 3000 years later.
flechal: The Flechal site (AM-MC-37) on the lower Madeira (Amazonas): one date of this time — 7320 ± 100 radiocarbon years (≈ 8100 cal years ago).
moxos-6000: Llanos de Moxos (Bolivia): people create forest islands from ≈ 10,850 cal years ago; squash ≈ 10,250, manioc ≈ 10,350 cal years ago — the oldest cultivation in Amazonia (Lombardo et al. 2020); ≈ 4700 artificial islands. Of this time — among others Isla 433 (7058 ± 50 radiocarbon years). To the east, on the Guaporé floodplain (Rondônia), — the Monte Castelo shell mound, the same kind of artificial mound of freshwater snail shells (Lombardo et al. 2013; Prestes-Carneiro et al. 2020): dates from ≈ 9300 to ≈ 700 cal years ago; of this time — 7010 ± 80 radiocarbon years (≈ 7960–7670 cal years ago).
moxos-8000: Llanos de Moxos (Bolivia): people create forest islands from ≈ 10,850 cal years ago; squash ≈ 10,250, manioc ≈ 10,350 cal years ago — the oldest cultivation in Amazonia (Lombardo et al. 2020); ≈ 4700 artificial islands. Apart, hundreds of kilometres of savanna away, — the islands Isla 493 "Lapis" (8920 ± 49 radiocarbon years) and Isla 575 "Hotel Caracoles" (8849 ± 50).
san-lucas: Site SL-79 in the San Lucas highlands (Chuquisaca, southern Bolivia): one date of this time — 7040 ± 60 radiocarbon years (≈ 7950–7700 cal years ago).
arq-18-6000: The ARQ-18 rockshelter in the Las Taguas valley (San Juan, 3760 m, by the main divide of the Andes; Marsh et al. 2016): component 4 — 8700–7600 cal years ago — the most intensive occupation of the shelter (hearths, ash pits). Tuina-type points — highland hunters from the north (the puna of Atacama and Jujuy). Then the shelter is empty for 1700 years, in the Middle Holocene drought (7600–5900 cal years ago).
arq-18-8000: The ARQ-18 rockshelter in the Las Taguas valley (San Juan, 3760 m, by the main divide of the Andes; Marsh et al. 2016): component 5 — 10,100–8700 cal years ago — rare visits of highland hunters; the first date is 8950 ± 100 radiocarbon years. Later, 8700–7600 cal years ago, comes the most intensive occupation of the shelter.
el-penoncito: El Peñoncito cave (northern San Juan, near Jagüé): hunter-gatherers; dates of 7470 ± 60 and 7080 ± 60 radiocarbon years (≈ 8250 and 7850 cal years ago).
los-morrillos: The Los Morrillos culture (after Gambier 1985): the Los Morrillos grottoes in the Ansilta range (Calingasta, San Juan); triangular points. Grotto 2 — 8255 ± 170, 7920 ± 120 and 6480 ± 130 radiocarbon years.
cordoba-6000: Hunter-gatherers of Córdoba: the El Alto 3 rockshelter in the Sierras Chicas (7108 ± 74 radiocarbon years) and the Arroyo El Gaucho 1 site on the plain, ≈ 140 km to the east (7160 ± 90) — one date of this time each (≈ 8000 cal years ago).
serra-talhada-10000: Serra da Capivara (Piauí) at the Pleistocene–Holocene boundary: Toca do Elias — a hearth of the main layer, AMS date 10,270 ± 35 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,050–11,800 cal years ago); Toca do João Leite — 10,800 … 10,400 (Itaparica industry); the Holocene layers of Boqueirão da Pedra Furada — 10,454 … 10,040; Toca de Cima do Pilão — 10,390 ± 80; Boa Vista I; the Toca dos Coqueiros burial — ≈ 11,300 cal years ago. The disputed Pleistocene layers of Pedra Furada do not belong to this map.
lajeado-10000: The middle Tocantins (Lajeado area): the open-air site Miracema do Tocantins 1 — seven dates of 10,530 … 9397 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,700–10,300 cal years ago), an unbroken series. A separate part of the zone, ≈ 600 km from the main one.
lajeado-8000: The middle Tocantins (Lajeado area): the open-air site Capivara 5 — 10,050 … 8980 ± 70 radiocarbon years (the last ≈ 10,200–9800 cal years ago); Miracema do Tocantins 1 (55 km away) — until 9397 ± 80. A separate part of the zone, ≈ 600 km from the main one.
penas-trampas: The Peñas de las Trampas 1.1 rockshelter in the high puna of Antofagasta de la Sierra (Catamarca): the oldest traces of people are ≈ 10,200 and 10,000 radiocarbon years old (≈ 11,800–11,500 cal years ago); later, ≈ 9100–8800 cal years ago, the dead were buried here. The first dates are about the map date.
agua-de-la-cueva-10000: Agua de la Cueva is a large arch-shaped rockshelter in the Mendoza Precordillera (2900 m, by the high Canota pampa grazed by guanacos): occupied from the Pleistocene–Holocene transition; of this time — 10,950 ± 90, 10,350 ± 220 and 10,240 ± 60 radiocarbon years (García 1999, 2003).
agua-de-la-cueva-8000: Agua de la Cueva is a large arch-shaped rockshelter in the Mendoza Precordillera (2900 m, by the high Canota pampa grazed by guanacos): its deep layers belong to the Early and Middle Holocene, 10,560–8180 cal years ago; of this time — 9210 ± 70, 8800 ± 70 and 8460 ± 100 radiocarbon years (García 2003, 2005).
tagua-tagua: Tagua Tagua 2 on the shore of the former Tagua Tagua lagoon (central Chile): a Paleoindian site with fishtail points and the butchering of a horse and a gomphothere (mastodon) — the same point culture as across the Andes. One date of this time — 10,120 ± 130 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,650 cal years ago; Núñez et al. 1994).
el-alto-3: The El Alto 3 rockshelter in the Sierras Chicas (Córdoba) — the oldest occupation of the Córdoba hills: dates of 11,010 ± 80 and 9790 ± 80 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,900 and 11,000 cal years ago; Prates et al. 2013).
marfilo: The Marfilo 1 rockshelter on the shore of Lake Calafquén (Araucanía, Chile): an Early Holocene occupation (Mera & García 2004); one date of this time — 10,190 ± 120 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,750 cal years ago); the next is ≈ 2400 years later.
cerro-casa-de-piedra: The Cerro Casa de Piedra 7 rockshelter in the Andes of Santa Cruz (near Perito Moreno): early occupations (Civalero & Aschero 2003) — 10,690 ± 72 radiocarbon years (on bone), then 9730 ± 100 and 9640 ± 64 (≈ 11,000 cal years ago).
nare: The Nare tradition: hunter-gatherers of the tropical forests of the Middle Magdalena valley (150–450 m) — La Palestina, San Juan de Bedout, Yondó; ≈ 10,400–10,230 radiocarbon years ago (≈ 12,600–11,500 cal). Triangular stemmed points of chert and white quartz, plano-convex scrapers.
porce: Early hunter-gatherers of the Porce valley (Antioquia, 850–1180 m): site PIII01-52 — 10,260 ± 50 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,400–11,800 cal years ago). Stone tools — hoe-axes, grinding stones and bifacial points of local white quartz; some sites of the middle Porce are residential camps. One date of this time.
arica-highlands-8000: The highland hunter-gatherer tradition of the Archaic of the south-central Andes (Osorio et al. 2017) — the dry puna east of Arica, 3100–4500 m: Hakenasa cave (18 dates of 9980 … 8340 radiocarbon years), the Las Cuevas rockshelter, the open-air site Ipilla 2 (15 AMS dates of 8940 … 8510), Pampa El Muerto 15, Quebrada La Higuera. Triangular and shouldered stemmed points (Patapatane type), scrapers; according to the authors — permanent life in the puna, not seasonal trips from the coast.
cerros-pintados: The Cerros Pintados 2 site on the edge of the Pampa del Tamarugal (Tarapacá): 9066 ± 80 and 8840 ± 90 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,200–9900 cal years ago) — early hunter-gatherers of the desert oases at the foot of the Andes.
chinchihuapi: Chinchihuapi I near Monte Verde (Llanquihue, Chile; Dillehay et al. 2019): besides the Late Pleistocene one, an Early Holocene occupation ≈ 10,000 cal years ago (8989 ± 74 radiocarbon years): small hearths, tools and debitage, two fragments of "Paiján-like" points.
abrigo-do-sol-8000: The Abrigo do Sol rockshelter (upper Guaporé, Mato Grosso): a continuous series of dates from ≈ 11,100 to ≈ 6500 cal years ago (Miller); of this time — 9245 ± 120, 9115 ± 160 and 8930 ± 100 radiocarbon years.
justino: The Justino necropolis on the São Francisco (Canindé de São Francisco, Sergipe): the oldest cemetery D — six burials of hunter-gatherers, 8950 ± 70 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,000 cal years ago). Later, potters buried their dead here for millennia. One date of this time.
abrigo-do-pilao: The Pilão rockshelter in central Bahia: 9650 ± 90 … 8790 ± 80 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,000–9800 cal years ago) — Early Holocene hunter-gatherers of the caatinga.
breu-branco: The open-air site Breu Branco 1 on the lower Tocantins (south-eastern Pará): 9570 ± 70 and 7940 ± 90 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,900 and 8750 cal years ago) — hunter-gatherers of the Amazon forest.
calima-8000: The Calima preceramic tradition (Salgado 1988–1990): the upper Calima — Sauzalito (9670 ± 150 … 9300 ± 100 radiocarbon years) and El Recreo (a buried soil — 8750 ± 160, the cultural layer — ≈ 7950–7850). A simple technology on river pebbles: hoe-axes with two side notches for hafting, grinding stones, hammerstones, flakes; no projectile points. Plant gathering, small game hunting, fishing. Different from the industries of the Sabana de Bogotá and the Magdalena; similar to Las Vegas (Ecuador).
el-abrigo-ica: The El Abrigo rockshelter in the Ica valley (southern Peru): 8835 ± 145 radiocarbon years (≈ 9900 cal years ago) — early hunter-gatherers of the coastal desert (excavated by F. Engel). One date of this time.
vermilion-lakes: The Vermilion Lakes site in the Bow valley near Banff (the Canadian Rockies; Fedje et al. 1995): at least six Paleoindian layers, ≈ 10,570 … 9570 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,500–10,900 cal years ago); windbreak shelters, perhaps bighorn sheep hunting — a mountain way of life, not steppe bison hunting.
western-colorado-10000: Paleoindians of the Western Slope of Colorado — the mountains and plateaus west of the Rockies: Kib Ridge–Yampa (Paleoindian layers 11,290 … 10,260 radiocarbon years), Eagle Rock Shelter on the Gunnison (more than 50 hearths; 10,970 … 10,300), the Folsom site of Mountaineer (until 10,295 ± 50), Black Mountain on the upper Rio Grande, NCY Ellen. The Mountaineer dates are 100–200 years later than the usual end of Folsom.
middle-atlantic-nesquehoning: Nesquehoning Creek (36CR142, Pennsylvania) — a Paleoindian site with fluted points: 10,480 ± 30, 10,340 ± 40 and 9940 ± 50 radiocarbon years (Stewart et al. 2018).
middle-atlantic-barton: The Barton site (18AG3) on the North Branch of the Potomac (Maryland): Clovis and Hardaway–Dalton in its assemblage; dates of 10,370 ± 50 and 9540 ± 50 radiocarbon years.
middle-atlantic-cactus-hill: Cactus Hill (44SX202) on the Nottoway River (Virginia): a Clovis layer ≈ 12,800 cal years ago; one date of this time — 10,160 ± 60 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,800 cal years ago).
peace-river-8000: Saskatoon Mountain (GhQt-4, Grande Prairie, Peace River country): a multi-layer Early Holocene site; dates of 9360 ± 60 and 8130 ± 130 radiocarbon years, then a series down to ≈ 5800.
colorado-plateau-8000: The Early Archaic of the Colorado Plateau: by the map date the stemmed points of the Paleoarchaic have already given way to notched ones (Pinto / Elko), and the first grinding stones appear (North Creek Shelter near Escalante, stratum V, from ≈ 9000 radiocarbon years; Janetski et al. 2012). Dust Devil Cave (Navajo Mountain) — coprolites with grass and goosefoot seeds, 8967 … 8751; Jim Walters Cave in Glen Canyon; on the Western Slope of Colorado — Eagle Rock Shelter, NCY Ellen and sites of La Plata County. Later, the Oshara tradition lives here.
plano-water-canyon: Water Canyon (Socorro, New Mexico) — a Bison antiquus bonebed: an Eden point among the bones, a Scottsbluff base — the Cody complex; dates of 9240 ± 50 … 8776 ± 62 radiocarbon years (Dello-Russo 2014, 2015).
serra-talhada-6000: The Serra Talhada phase in the Serra da Capivara (Piauí): 24 sites of 12,700–8000 years ago; burials and hearths ≈ 11,000–9500 cal years ago (Toca dos Coqueiros burial 11,390–11,170, Paraguaio 10,150–9430); Sítio do Meio, phase Serra Talhada I, ≈ 9400–8100 radiocarbon years. Baixa das Cabaceiras is one of these sites. The disputed Pleistocene layers of Pedra Furada are not part of this map.
nostvet-lihult-6000: Nøstvet–Lihult: the Late Mesolithic of south-eastern Norway and western Sweden — the Skagerrak coast from Lista to Göteborg, the lowland around the Oslofjord and the shores of Lake Vänern with Värmland. Nøstvet begins c. 6300 BC (ground axes, microliths); in western Sweden the map date falls at the change from the Sandarna to the Lihult culture (c. 5900 BC). Sites dated to this time — Skoklefall, Kvestad, Krøgenes, Ullern (Norway), Gunnarsröd, Ödsmål, Kvernos, Vestanvik (Sweden).
west-norway-6000: Late Mesolithic of western Norway (c. 6500–4000 BC): sea-mammal hunters and fishers of the coast and fjords from Lista to Lofoten; their bone technology is of the "eastern" kind. Sites dated to this time — Kotedalen (Nordhordland), Sævarhelleren in the Hardangerfjord, Viste cave (Randaberg), Botten (Karmøy).
norway-uplands-6000: Mesolithic of the uplands and valleys of southern Norway: seasonal camps of reindeer hunters — Vrålsbu (Hardangervidda), Hovatn (Agder heights), Mørstadstølen (Valdres), Dokkfløyvatn, Persmyrkoia (Rena valley). No separate "culture" is defined here: people from both the west coast and the east came up to these hunting grounds.
motala-6000: Late Mesolithic at the outlet of the Motala ström from Lake Vättern: the sites of Kanaljorden, Strandvägen, Verkstadsvägen and Alvastra. People were here from c. 9000 BC, but the Late Mesolithic settlements on the river were founded around 5800 BC, when the river cut through its threshold again; the map date is at the very beginning.
gotland-6000: Seal hunters of Gotland: the island was settled c. 7250 BC; sites — Mölner (Väte parish) and Stora Förvar cave on Stora Karlsö. Unlike the mainland: an island tradition of its own.
kalmar-strait-6000: Late Mesolithic of the shores of the Kalmar Strait and south-western Öland: Tingby, Hässlehult (Ryssby), Alby. Kristianstad flint, porphyry, transverse arrowheads, rare Lihult axes; the Kalmar Mesolithic has features of its own compared with its neighbours.
kunda-6000: Kunda culture: hunters and fishers of Estonia, Latvia, northern Lithuania and north-western Russia — from the north coast of Estonia (Jägala, Kuusalu) to western Latvia (Sise on the Užava, 6210–5000 BC). In north-western Saaremaa (Võhma, Pahapilli) the first dates are around 5800 BC. Around 5400–5300 BC it is replaced by the Narva culture with pottery.
ireland-6000: Later Mesolithic of Ireland: heavy blades and "Bann flakes" (after the river Bann), found only in Ireland and on the Isle of Man. Sites dated to this time — Mount Sandel and Newferry (Bann valley), Larne, Ringneill (Strangford Lough), Dalkey Island and Sutton (Dublin), Lullymore, Gortore (Cork). The Isle of Man belongs to the same circle, but its nearest dated finds are c. 7500 and c. 5700 BC.
teviec-6000: Téviecian culture: the Late Mesolithic of southern Brittany (c. 6200–5000 BC). Shell middens and burials on the islands of Téviec and Hoedic (the first Hoedic burials 6081–5985 BC), the sites of Beg-er-Vil, Le Souc'h, Quélarn and Port-Neuf on Hoedic.
janislawice-6000: Janisławice (Nemunas) culture: the Late Mesolithic of Lithuania, eastern Poland, Belarus and Ukrainian Polesia — rhomboid and trapezoid microliths; Lithuanian authors write "Nemunas (Janisławice)". The Donkalnis and Spiginas burials at Lake Biržulis (6660–5790 BC), the sites of Nieborowa, Rydno, Merkinė, Jonionys, Zagorye-2, Kalinino. Neman pottery comes later, from c. 5000 BC.
sado-mira-6000: Shell middens and cemeteries of the Sado estuary (Arapouco, Vale de Romeiras, Amoreiras, Cabeço do Pez) and the lower Mira (Fiais): the same circle as Muge, c. 6500–5700 BC, on the Sado into the 5th millennium.
algarve-6000: Late Mesolithic of the western Algarve: the shell middens of Vale Boi and Castelejo near Cape St Vincent — from c. 7800 to 4800 BC without a break; pottery from c. 5500 BC.
cocina-6000: Geometric Mesolithic of eastern Iberia (Cocina facies): trapezes and triangles; Valencia, Alicante and Lower Aragon. Sites dated to this time — Cocina, Tossal de la Roca, Falguera, Ballester, Casa Corona (Villena), Botiquería and Costalena (Aragon). The Cardial Neolithic arrives c. 5600 BC.
upper-ebro-6000: Geometric Mesolithic of the upper Ebro and the western Pyrenees: Aizpea (Navarre), Atxoste, Mendandia and Fuente Hoz (Álava), Forcas (Huesca), La Margineda (Andorra). At La Margineda the last Mesolithic dates are around 6100 BC, the Neolithic begins c. 5400 BC.
castelnovian-6000: Castelnovian culture — the "second" Mesolithic with trapezes of south-eastern France and northern Italy (c. 6800–5500 BC): Languedoc and Provence (Châteauneuf-les-Martigues — the eponym, Montclus, Hortus), the Rhône valley and the Northern Alps, Liguria, the Northern Apennines, Trentino, Friuli, the Trieste karst, Ljubljana (Breg), the Dolomites (Plan de Frea, Mondeval de Sora). Separately — the Fucino basin (Abruzzo) and northern Calabria and Basilicata (Grotta della Madonna, Latronico). On the coast the Impressa begins c. 5850 BC, in the Po plain the Neolithic c. 5300 BC.
uzzo-6000: Late Mesolithic of western Sicily: Grotta dell'Uzzo (Zingaro reserve) — a Mesolithic passing without a break into the Neolithic (cereals from c. 5650 BC, then the Stentinello culture), Grotta d'Oriente on Favignana, Cala dei Genovesi on Levanzo.
impressa-apulia-6000: Early Neolithic with Impressed Ware in south-eastern Italy: the first farming villages of the Tavoliere, the Murge and the Salento — Lagnano da Piede, Pulo di Molfetta, Scamuso, Trasano, Torre Sabea, the flint mines of Defensola (Gargano); c. 6100–5600 BC.
impressa-adriatic-6000: Early Neolithic with Impressed Ware on the eastern shore of the Adriatic: Istria (Medulin), Dalmatia and its islands (Pokrovnik, Crno Vrilo, Zemunica, Grapčeva, Vela Špilja, Gudnja), Montenegro (Vruća), Corfu (Sidari), southern Albania (Konispol); c. 6000–5500 BC. In the mountains of Montenegro (Odmut cave) the map date shows a Mesolithic passing into the Neolithic.
starcevo-6000: Starčevo–Criş: the first farmers of Serbia, Vojvodina, the Banat, Transylvania, Oltenia, Slavonia and Bosnia (c. 6100–5400 BC). Sites dated to this time — Starčevo, Blagotin, Drenovac, Divostin, Donja Branjevina (Serbia), Gura Baciului, Seuşa, Miercurea Sibiului, Foeni (Romania), Galovo (Croatia), Obre (Bosnia). On the Hungarian plain the Körös begins later, c. 5800 BC.
karanovo-6000: Karanovo I: the Early Neolithic of Bulgaria and Aegean Thrace (c. 6100–5800 BC) — painted pottery, tell settlements. Sites dated to this time — Azmak, Chavdar, Galabnik, Kovačevo, Dzhulyunitsa (Bulgaria), Dikili Tash, Sidirokastro, Limenaria on Thasos, Makri (Greece).
thessaly-6000: Early Neolithic of Thessaly and central Greece (proto-Sesklo): the settlements of Sesklo, Achilleion, Theopetra, Mavropigi and Varemenoi (Western Macedonia), Elateia and Chaironeia, Schisto cave (Attica), Franchthi (Argolid; the Neolithic here from c. 6800 BC). Around 5800 BC the Middle Neolithic — the Sesklo culture — begins.
anzabegovo-6000: Early Neolithic of North Macedonia: Anzabegovo and Vršnik-Tarinci (Ovče Pole), Veluška (Pelagonia); painted pottery, links with Thessaly and Karanovo.
nea-nikomedeia-6000: Nea Nikomedeia (Imathia plain): one of the oldest farming villages in Europe, Early Neolithic from c. 6400 BC; a large "central" house, clay figurines.
turkish-thrace-6000: Neolithic of European Turkey and the Marmara coast: Hoca Çeşme near the mouth of the Maritsa, Yarımburgaz, Yenikapı (Istanbul, the oldest layers — Neolithic burials and houses); close to the Fikirtepe culture of the Asian shore. On the Asian shore — Ilıpınar, Barcın and Menteşe (the İznik and Yenişehir basins) and Aktopraklık near Bursa: their dates cover the date of the map.
knossos-6000: Early Neolithic of Crete: Knossos — the aceramic Neolithic (stratum X, c. 7000 BC) and the Early Neolithic without a break; the island's first farmers came by sea.
maroulas-6000: Mesolithic of the Cyclades: the site of Maroulas near Loutra on Kythnos — round huts and burials of hunter-gatherers who sailed to the islands; abandoned in the mid-6th millennium BC.
dniester-bug-6000: Late Mesolithic of the Dniester and Southern Bug: the Grebeniki culture (Budjak, the lower Dniester — Mirnoe, Grebeniki) and the early Bug–Dniester (Soroca, Sokol'tsy II, Pechera). At the map date it is still a Mesolithic world; the local hunters adopt pottery at the beginning of the 6th millennium BC.
murzak-koba-6000: Murzak-Koba culture of Mountain Crimea: the map date is its late stage (Shan-Koba, layer 3 — 6056–5842 BC; the burial in Fatma-Koba); around 5900 BC it is followed by the Neolithic Tash-Air culture.
rakushechny-yar-6000: Rakushechny Yar culture: the Early Neolithic of the lower Don — the multi-layered settlement of Rakushechny Yar (an island near Razdorskaya) and Matveev Kurgan on the Mius.
middle-don-6000: Middle Don culture — the Early Neolithic of the middle Bityug (Monastyrskaya 1, Shchuchye 2). Its beginning is put "at the turn of the 7th and 6th millennia BC", but the early age of this pottery is disputed: it is fully decorated from the start. In the second half of the 6th millennium the culture covers the whole Voronezh region.
serteya-6000: Serteya culture (c. 7000–5300 BC): hunters and fishers of the Dnieper–Dvina interfluve — the Serteya, Usvyaty and Sennitsa micro-regions; one of the early pottery traditions of the forest zone (pottery from the 7th millennium BC).
elshanka-6000: Elshanka culture — the Early Neolithic of the forest-steppe Volga region (the Samara, Sok and Bolshoy Cheremshan): Ivanovskaya, Staroelshanka, Chekalino IV, Lebyazhinka IV. It begins around the map date (c. 6100–5875 BC); the Middle Volga culture later grows out of it.
vozhe-6000: Mesolithic and Early Neolithic of the Lake Vozhe basin (Vologda region): Pogostishche 15 — a Mesolithic of 7800–7100 BC, Karavaikha 4 — 6390–4624 BC; continuity between the Mesolithic and the Neolithic here is debated.
orlovka-6000: Orlovka culture — the Early Neolithic of the Saratov trans-Volga region and the Volga–Ural interfluve (c. 6250–4500 BC): Algai, Oroshaemoe, Varfolomeevka; pottery with stab-and-drag decoration.
kairshak-6000: Kairshak (Kairshak–Tentyaksor) culture — the Early Neolithic of the northern Caspian: Kairshak III (6230–5720 BC), Baibek; pottery decorated with incised lines. Typologically the oldest are Kugat IV and Kulagaisy (the south of the Volga–Ural sands): dates on pottery — the middle of the 7th millennium BC (Vybornov et al. 2020).
shulaveri-6000: Shulaveri–Shomutepe culture: the first farmers and herders of the Kura and Khrami valleys (c. 6000–5300 BC), round mud-brick houses — Gadachrili Gora, Arukhlo (Georgia), Hacı Elamxanlı, Kiçik Tepe, Damjili (Azerbaijan). It begins around 6000 BC.
kultepe-6000: Kültepe culture of Nakhchivan: the settlement of Kültepe I — an Early Neolithic with dates of 6372–5836 BC.
aratashen-6000: Aratashen culture — the Early Neolithic of the Ararat plain: Aratashen, Aknashen, Masis Blur; it begins around the map date ("around 6000 BC or slightly earlier").
chokh-6000: Chokh culture — the Neolithic of mountain Dagestan: the settlement of Chokh (Neolithic layer c. 6050–6010 BC), with a Mesolithic below it from the 11th millennium BC.
bertheaume-8000: The Bertheaume group — the Early ("first") Mesolithic of western Brittany: narrow backed bladelets; the sites of Toul-an-Naouac'h (Plougoulm), Quillien (Le Cloître-Saint-Thégonnec), Le Bilou (Le Conquet). The second Mesolithic of Brittany — the Téviecian — comes later, from c. 6000 BC.
cyclops-8000: Mesolithic of the Northern Sporades: the Cave of Cyclops on Youra — hunter-gatherers and fishers who caught tuna; one of the few Mesolithic sites of the Aegean islands.
belloisian: Long-blade industries of the Somme basin ("Belloisian"): sites with large blades with battered edges — Belloy-sur-Somme, Hangest-sur-Somme, Saleux, Conty, in the west — Le Buhot (Eure); the end of the Younger Dryas — beginning of the Preboreal. A similar industry in England — Sproughton.
epigravettian-istria: Final Epigravettian of the eastern Adriatic shore: the caves of Pupićina (Istria), Šandalja II (Pula), Vlakno on Dugi Otok; occupied in both the Bølling–Allerød and the Younger Dryas.
epigravettian-epirus: Final Epigravettian of Epirus: the rockshelters of Klithi (Voidomatis gorge) and Boila (near Konitsa) — hunters of ibex and chamois; Boila continues Klithi.
estebanvela: Late Magdalenian and Azilian of the northern Meseta: the cave of Peña de Estebanvela on the northern slope of the Sierra de Ayllón (Segovia) — a series of dates without a break from the Late Magdalenian to the Azilian.
fariseu: Final Magdalenian of the Côa valley: the site of Fariseu — layers of the end of the Magdalenian and the Azilian with engravings on stone, next to the famous rock engravings of the Côa valley.
nerja-10000: Epimagdalenian of Málaga: Nerja Cave — occupied both before and after the map date; the last reliable dates of this period are around 12,300 years ago.
diablets: Microlaminar Epipalaeolithic of northern Valencia: the Diablets rockshelter (Alcalà de Xivert) — an industry of tiny bladelets, the same as at Santa Maira.
zolotoruchye: Zolotoruchye tradition of the Upper Volga: the site of Zolotoruchye 1 near Uglich, the lower complex — the beginning of the Younger Dryas; according to M. G. Zhilin, proto-Butovo.
early-khartoum-8000: Early Khartoum (c. 8500–5000 BC), at the confluence of the Blue and White Nile (Khartoum, Sarourab, El Khiday) and at the Sixth Cataract (the Sphinx site at Jebel Sabaloka, c. 10,700–10,500 cal BP): fishers and gatherers with early 'wavy line' pottery. Downstream, at the mouth of the Atbara — Abu Darbein, fishers with the same pottery (c. 9,650–9,350 cal BP).
nemrikian: Early villages in the foothills of northern Iraq: round semi-subterranean houses, hunting and gathering of wild cereals. Nemrik 9 — c. 9800–8270 BC; the culture is thought to grow out of the Zarzian. The map date is at its beginning.
bolaghi-10000: Sites of the Bolaghi valley (upper Pulvar), excavated before the Sivand dam was built; the oldest dates are c. 12,000 years ago.
pigeon-mountain: Pigeon Mountain (Qingtongxia) on the Yellow River: camps with microblades and grinding stones of the northern Chinese "Mesolithic", c. 13,000–9,000 years ago.
sagan-nuge: Sagan-Nuge on the western shore of Lake Baikal, opposite Olkhon Island: a final Palaeolithic camp, c. 12,200–11,800 cal BP. A new AMS date of layer XI: 12,100–11,750 cal BP (OxA-34599).
denisova-10000: The entrance zone of Denisova Cave (Anui valley): final Palaeolithic layers, c. 13,100–11,900 cal BP. Nearby Kaminnaya Cave has layers of about the same time.
tibesti-8000: Valleys of the north-western Tibesti (Enneri Tabi, Enneri Dirennao): early Holocene hunter-gatherers, dates c. 11,000–8,600 cal BP. To the north, at Serir Tibesti, one date of about the same time.
termit-8000: Termit West (Niger): early pottery of the Termit massif, c. 10,600–9,400 cal BP.
ouargla-8000: Ouargla basin: camps by the early Holocene lakes (Sebkha Mellala, Hassi Mouillah). Hassi Mouillah has the earliest dates of the Mellalian culture: backed bladelets, denticulates, decorated ostrich eggshell, c. 10,100–9,300 cal BP.
tinrhert-8000: Izimane on the Tinrhert plateau, north of the Tassili: two dates, c. 11,200 and c. 9,000 cal BP.
ouled-nail-8000: Aïn Naga in the Ouled Naïl mountains (Saharan Atlas): early layers of the Upper Capsian — geometric microliths, ostrich eggshell, c. 10,400–9,700 cal BP.
tshitolian-8000: The Tshitolian industry: hunter-gatherers of the forest-savanna mosaic with leaf-shaped and trapeze arrowheads. Malebo Pool (Gombe Point, Kabu 4 in Kinshasa) and Ngongo Mbata in the lower Congo; dates c. 11,000–8,600 cal BP.
mouanko-8000: Mouanko-Lobethal at the Sanaga estuary (Cameroon): Later Stone Age, two dates c. 10,000 and c. 9,600 cal BP.
chicaza-8000: Chicaza rockshelter (Niassa, northern Mozambique): Later Stone Age, dates c. 10,300 and c. 9,300 cal BP.
vanderlin-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Wobuya rockshelter on Vanderlin Island (c. 8000–7800 cal BP; shell dates corrected for the marine reservoir) and Mushroom Rock. On the date of the map Vanderlin is still part of the mainland coast; it becomes an island c. 6700 years ago, after which people almost leave until c. 4200 years ago.
urumbal-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Urumbal Pocket on the Atherton Tableland (charcoal c. 8400–7900 cal BP): people visited the rainforest from the early Holocene, but settled it fully only in the last c. 2000 years.
nara-inlet-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Nara Inlet 1 rockshelter on Hook Island: dates of c. 9000 and c. 7500 years ago — before and after the date of the map. The island was then probably still joined to the mainland or just separating.
youlain-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Youlain Springs in the Paroo basin (south-west Queensland): charcoal c. 9500–8400 and c. 7200–6700 cal BP — before and after the date of the map.
