The site is by springs between the Paroo and Bulloo rivers (Robins 1998); nearby, tools lie in a layer with a TL date of c. 7900 years.
nullarbor-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Allen's Cave: dates of c. 9000 and c. 6000 years ago, with no dates in between.
new-ireland-6000: Ancestors of the Papuans. The island was never joined to New Guinea. Matenbek and Buang Merabak caves on the east coast and Balof 2 in the north: hunting of the cuscus, gathering of shellfish; obsidian was brought from New Britain. Panakiwuk cave is abandoned by this time.
psytuaje-10000: Epipalaeolithic hunters of the North Caucasus (their languages are unknown). Psytuaje rockshelter — a camp of hunters of the Caucasian tur, dated c. 11,800 and c. 11,300 years ago; obsidian came from Zayukovo, 6–7 km away. In the nearby Sosruko rockshelter, layers run from c. 17,000 to c. 9000 years ago: here the culture went on without a break from the Ice Age into the early Holocene.
baume-loire-10000: The last Magdalenians of the upper Loire (their languages are unknown). The Baume-Loire rockshelters near Solignac-sur-Loire — a date of c. 11,900 years ago; in rockshelter 2 this level lies above a layer of fallen blocks of the Younger Dryas. The tools are small and made only of local flint; unlike the neighbouring Allier valley, there are no Azilian points here. Soon Mesolithic hunters with geometric microliths will appear here (Longetraye).
ayamaru-10000: Ancestors of the Papuans. Toé Cave by the Ayamaru lakes in the centre of the Bird's Head: cassowary eggshell, brought into the cave by people, c. 11,900–11,300 years ago; people came to the plateau from c. 24,000 years ago.
puntutjarpa-10000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Puntutjarpa rockshelter by the Warburton Range: the first occupation, c. 12,000–9700 years ago (Smith et al. 2017); charcoal near the base — c. 12,600–11,200 years ago.
golyi-mys-10000: A camp of Final Palaeolithic hunters on the lower Amur (Golyi Mys IV); the last traces are c. 12,200 years ago. Its stone industry differs from the Osipovka culture upstream.
psytuaje-8000: Epipalaeolithic hunters and gatherers of the North Caucasus (their languages are unknown). Sosruko rockshelter — dates c. 10,100 and c. 9800 years ago: edible snails were gathered and eaten here (thousands of shells), tur, deer and wild boar were hunted; Psytuaje rockshelter — c. 10,200 years ago. About 8500 years ago a pottery Neolithic will appear here.
dvoinaya-8000: Late Mesolithic hunters of the north-western Caucasus (their languages are unknown). Dvoinaya Cave and Chygai rockshelter in the Gubs gorge — dates c. 10,700–9500 years ago. Bladelets were made by pressure flaking, a difficult technique not known here before; it was probably brought by newcomers. The bladelets were used as inserts for arrowheads.
ayamaru-8000: Ancestors of the Papuans. Toé Cave by the Ayamaru lakes in the centre of the Bird's Head: cassowary eggshell brought by people, c. 10,200–9600 years ago; hunters of the forest wallaby lived on the plateau from c. 24,000 years ago.
puntutjarpa-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Puntutjarpa rockshelter by the Warburton Range: the first occupation, c. 12,000–9700 years ago, then a break until c. 8300 years ago (Smith et al. 2017).
baikal-shore-8000: Mesolithic of the western shore of Lake Baikal: multi-layer sites near Olkhon and Buguldeika (Ityrkhei I, Berloga, Sagan-Nuge, Buguldeika II) — hunters of hoofed animals and the Baikal seal; layers c. 10,800–8500 years ago.
kamchatka-8000: Initial Neolithic of Kamchatka (c. 9900–8600 years ago): hunters with prismatic cores and blade tools lived in surface tents by Ushki Lake and in the Anavgai valley (Ushki I, layer V; Anavgai II; Razdelny I).
ayamaru-6000: Ancestors of the Papuans. Kria and Toé caves by the Ayamaru lakes: hunters of the forest wallaby (djief) lived here from c. 24,000 years ago; Kria Cave — from c. 8000 years ago.
badu-6000: Ancestors of the Torres Strait Islanders and Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Badu was then still hills at the edge of Cape York; people lived here permanently c. 8000–6000 years ago (David et al. 2004).
puntutjarpa-6000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Puntutjarpa rockshelter by the Warburton Range: people return here c. 8300 years ago after a break; the richest mid-Holocene layer in the Australian deserts (Smith et al. 2017).
trans-urals-6000: The first potters of the Trans-Urals: pointed- and round-based vessels with pricked and incised patterns (Koshkino and Kozlovo traditions), rectangular pit houses, hunting and fishing. On Lake Yurinskoe the sanctuary of Koksharovsky Hill is built from c. 6400 BC; on the Ishim (Mergen 6), next to Koshkino pottery, there is flat-based early Boborykino ware (Mosin 2024).
baraba-6000: Early Neolithic of the Baraba forest-steppe: flat-based pottery, storage pits for fermented fish and a ritual complex on the Tartas; dates — 7th millennium BC, running into the 6th (Molodin et al. 2020).
wsib-taiga-6000: Taiga hunter-fishers with the first pottery (pricked, flat- and round-based) build the northernmost fortified settlements of Eurasia — Amnya I on the Kazym, Kayukovo 2 on the Salym, Mikishkino 5 at Barsova Gora near Surgut (c. 6000 BC); on the Konda — the cemetery of Bolshaya Umytya 100, where Neolithic graves continue the rows of Mesolithic ones (Klementyeva, Pogodin 2020).
satyga-6000: The Satyga type at the foot of the Northern Urals: pit houses on the shore of Lake Nizhnee, flat-based pottery with applied ridges; the settlement was used from c. 6600 to c. 5500 BC (Chairkina, Dubovtseva 2016).
yenisei-6000: The first pottery on the Middle Yenisei: in Eleneva Cave near Krasnoyarsk, horizon 11G with cord- and comb-impressed pottery lies directly on the Mesolithic layers; date c. 5800 BC (Makarov).
chikoi-6000: Early Neolithic of the Chikoi valley: burials of hunters and fishers — Zhindo, Ust-Menza 5, Melnichnoe (c. 8000–7600 years ago, dated on the bones of the buried); the dead lie flexed, sprinkled with ochre. Settlements of the same time are not yet dated.
ust-karenga-6000: Hunter-gatherers of the upper Vitim with pottery; the uppermost layer of the culture at Ust-Karenga III — c. 8100–7800 years ago; here the culture lasts until c. 7500 years ago.
middle-vitim-6000: Burials under stone cairns on the middle Vitim — Nizhnyaya Dzhilinda and Staryi Vitim II near Ust-Muya (c. 8100–8000 years ago, dated on the bones of the buried): nephrite knives, beads, inset daggers.
sumnagin-6000: Mesolithic hunters and fishers of Yakutia (Sumnagin culture): microblades and inset tools, conical cores, adzes. Shown by the sites of the Aldan and the Middle Lena (Ust-Timpton, Sumnagin I, Belkachi I); here the culture lasts until c. 6800 years ago, then it is replaced by the Syalakh culture with the first pottery.
east-chukotka-6000: Reindeer hunters with microblade tools in the east of Chukotka — Naivan I on the Bering Sea coast (dates 9000–7000 years ago with a large error) and the lower layer of Ulkhum (c. 7700 years ago); they are assigned to the Sumnagin circle.
lower-amur-6000: Fishers and hunters of the Lower Amur with flat-based pottery and prismatic cores. Around 6000 BC, settlements are dated here at Suchu (near Mariinskoe), Malaya Gavan and in the lower layer of Sakachi-Alyan. I. Ya. Shevkomud assigns them to the early stage of the Kondon culture, V. E. Medvedev to the Mariinsky and early Malyshevo cultures.
rudnaya-6000: The early pottery of Primorye — flat-based vessels with rhombic stamp impressions ("Amur weave"); pit houses, bow and arrows, fishing and hunting. Around 6000 BC the early Rudnaya stage (Rudnaya Pristan, Luzanova Sopka 2) gives way to the Sergeevka stage (Novotroitskoe 2, Ustinovka 8, Chertovy Vorota). In Chertovy Vorota cave charred mats and textiles have survived.
orlinyi-klyuv-6000: Hunters and fishers of the middle Bolshaya Ussurka (Iman) with flat-based pottery; at Orlinyi Klyuv — a dwelling dated c. 8000 years ago. V. A. Lynsha distinguishes the Orlinyi Klyuv culture here; other researchers see it as a local variant of the Rudnaya or Kondon culture.
yarmukian-6000: Yarmukian culture and Jericho IX (Lodian) — the Early Pottery Neolithic of the southern Levant (c. 6400–5800 BC; Banning 2007): Sha'ar HaGolan, Munhata, 'Ain Ghazal, Nahal Qanah cave; Jericho, Lod, Dhra'. The first pottery, incised pebbles and figurines; farmers and herders. The Yarmukian ends c. 5990–5760 BC; then comes the Wadi Rabah culture.
black-desert-6000: Late Neolithic of the Black Desert (north-eastern Jordan): Wisad Pools, Burqu, Dhuweila — dates c. 6100–5900 BC. Round and oval stone houses and pens, gazelle hunting with "desert kites", the first sheep and goats. A complex of hunter-herders rather than one "culture" (Wasse et al. 2024; Betts 1993).
timnian-6000: Early Timnian — the first herders of the Negev: Ramon I rockshelter (a layer of goat dung, c. 6200–5800 BC), Nahal Issaron, Shunera. Small camps with round structures and pens, tabular scrapers; goats and sheep alongside hunting and gathering. The Timnian complex lasts until the 3rd millennium BC (Rosen 2016; Avner 2018).
dfbw-6000: Pottery Neolithic of the northern Levant and Cilicia — the circle of Dark Faced Burnished Ware (c. 7000–5800 BC): Byblos, Ras Shamra, the Amuq (Tell Kurdu), the Rouj basin (Tell el-Kerkh, already with Proto-Halaf pottery), Yumuktepe (Mersin). In the Bekaa valley — surveyed sites of this time; at Ard Tlaili the Late Neolithic begins at about the date of the map.
proto-halaf-6000: Proto-Halaf — a short transition to the Halaf culture, c. 6100–5950 BC (Cruells, Nieuwenhuyse 2004): Sabi Abyad, Halula, Chagar Bazar, Kazane, Mezraa-Teleilat. Next to coarse ware appears a thin painted "Fine Ware"; rectangular houses, seals. Domuztepe (the west of the zone) is dated from c. 5985–5818 BC and already to the Early Halaf; its earliest layer is not dated.
hassuna-6000: Hassuna culture — early farmers of northern Mesopotamia (c. 6500–5900 BC): Hassuna, Yarim Tepe I, Sotto, Shimshara, the upper levels of Jarmo. Painted and incised pottery, houses of packed mud, granaries. At Yarim Tepe I the transition to "standard" Hassuna is dated c. 6016–5899 BC; nearby (Yarim Tepe II, Arpachiyah) the Halaf begins at about the date of the map.
hakemi-use-6000: Hakemi Use (upper Tigris, Bismil): a village of the "Hassuna–Samarra" Late Neolithic, five building levels, c. 6100–5950 BC; Samarra painting only in the upper levels (Tekin 2020; Petrova, Tekin 2023). Between it and the Sinjar plain lie c. 200 km without known sites.
samarra-6000: Samarra culture (c. 6200–5700 BC): Tell es-Sawwan on the middle Tigris and Choga Mami on the Diyala — the first irrigation canals, houses of mud brick, painted pottery of the "Samarra" style.
baghuz-6000: Tell Baghuz (Middle Euphrates near Abu Kemal): a short-lived village with "classic" Samarra painted pottery, by its style contemporary with the transitional period of Sabi Abyad (c. 6100–5950 BC). There are no radiocarbon dates — the date rests on the likeness of the pottery (Nieuwenhuyse 1999).
oueili-6000: Ubaid 0 — the oldest known level of southern Iraq, Tell el-Oueili near Larsa (c. 6500–5950 BC; Huot 1996): large mud-brick houses, granaries. Dated only by shells of lake molluscs; after this phase the village was abandoned for a long time — Ubaid 1 comes after a gap.
konya-6000: Late Neolithic and Early Chalcolithic of the Konya plain: Çatalhöyük East (its last levels — about 6000 BC) and West (Early Chalcolithic, painted pottery), Can Hasan I, Pınarbaşı B. Mud-brick houses entered through the roof, wall paintings.
aegean-6000: Neolithic of the Aegean coast of Anatolia: Ulucak, Ege Gübre, Çukuriçi (from İzmir to Ephesus), c. 6800–5700 BC. Farming villages with houses of packed mud and mud brick, red burnished pottery; links with the Aegean and the Balkans.
hajji-firuz-6000: Hajji Firuz culture — the Late Neolithic of the Lake Urmia basin (c. 6100–5500 BC): Hajji Firuz, Yanik Tepe. Square mud-brick houses, painted pottery; jars from Hajji Firuz hold one of the oldest traces of wine.
qazvin-6000: Early Neolithic of the Qazvin plain: Tepe Chahar Boneh — its dates cover the date of the map (Pollard 2011). The neighbouring Zagheh and Ebrahimabad are later than the window. At the edge of the window: Tepe Sialk North (the Late Neolithic I begins by the model c. 6015 BC; Pollard et al. 2013) and Tepe Khaleseh near Zanjan (by pottery 6000–5600 BC) — they are not on the map.
fars-6000: Neolithic of Fars (the Marv Dasht plain near Persepolis): Tall-e Mushki, Tall-e Jari B, Tol-e Bashi — dates c. 6200–5900 BC (Nishiaki 2010; Marshall 2012). Villages of the first farmers and herders with painted pottery. In the north-east, in the Bavanat valley (2364 m), — Hormangan, a Mushki–Jari village with dates near the date of the map (Khanipour et al. 2021). In Mamasani, Tol-e Nurabad begins just after it (early Jari painted pottery; Weeks et al. 2006).
jeitun-6000: Jeitun culture — the first farmers of Central Asia (c. 6300–4800 BC). About 6000 BC — two clusters of villages at the foot of the Kopet Dag: around Jeitun and Geok Tepe (Chopan, Togolok) and in the south-east, near Meana and Chaacha (Monjukli Depe, Chagylly); further west, as far as Bami, Jeitun villages appear later. One-room houses of clay blocks with a hearth, barley and wheat, goats and sheep.
xinglongwa-6000: Xinglongwa culture (c. 6200–5400 BC): the Xiliao basin — Aohan and Chifeng (Xinglongwa, Xinglonggou), Chahai near Fuxin. Villages of pit-houses in rows, surrounding ditches, jade ornaments, millet at Xinglonggou. In the west, on the upper Xilamulun, — villages of the Baiyinchahan type (Linxi). In Fuxin about 6000 BC lived also people of the Xiaohexi phase (Jiajiagou-Xi): small oval dwellings, coarse pottery with almost no decoration, stone spades.
jiahu-6000: Jiahu (Wuyang) — a village of the Peiligang circle of its own type (c. 7000–5800 BC): bone flutes, early rice, signs on turtle shells.
cishan-6000: Cishan culture (c. 6500–5000 BC): the Taihang foothills in southern Hebei and northern Henan — Cishan, Huawo. Storage pits with millet, grinding slabs, pigs and dogs.
beifudi-6000: Beifudi (Yishui, Hebei) — a village of c. 6000 BC with pit-houses and carved clay masks; related to Cishan and Xinglongwa.
houli-6000: Houli culture (c. 6500–5500 BC): northern Shandong at the foot of the Taishan mountains — Houli, Xihe, Yuezhuang. Large pit-houses, cooking pots; early rice and millet at Yuezhuang and Xihe.
kuahuqiao-6000: Kuahuqiao culture (c. 6000–5000 BC; Hangzhou Bay): Kuahuqiao, Xiaohuangshan. Pile dwellings, the oldest dugout canoe in China, rice, a lacquered bow. Also the Jingtoushan shell midden near Yuyao on the shore of Hangzhou Bay (c. 8300–7800 years ago), with the oldest wooden paddles and lacquerware in China; its excavators consider it a probable ancestor of the Hemudu culture.
pengtoushan-6000: Pengtoushan and Lower Zaoshi culture (c. 7000–5800 BC; the Liyang plain in northern Hunan): Bashidang, Hujiawuchang, Zaoshi. Ditches and banks around villages, early rice, thick pottery tempered with rice husk.
donets-middle-6000: Early Neolithic of the Middle Seversky Donets (Kleshnya type / early Donetsk culture): camps on the pine terraces and old channels of the Donets — Kleshnya 2, 3, 5, Kaidashchino 8 (Kreminna), Bondarikha II (Izium); by the excavators — the middle to third quarter of the 7th millennium BC. There is one direct date — a burial near Kleshnya 3, c. 6400–6050 BC (its link with the camp is disputed). The developed Donetsk culture belongs to the first half of the 6th millennium (the Zelena Hornytsia dates may be too young).
donets-lower-6000: Lower Seversky Donets: camps of the Donetsk culture Ust-Bystraya and Nizhneserebryakovskoe 1. The Early Neolithic here is placed by relative chronology (Tsybriy 2005: the middle of the 7th — first quarter of the 6th millennium BC); there are no radiocarbon dates of its own, and the sites are placed by district.
el-prodigio-6000: El Prodigio (El Limón, Chaparral, southern Tolima): an open-air site on a ridge of the eastern slope of the Central Cordillera (800–1000+ m) with a dark anthropogenic soil. Small flakes of chert and quartz of the "Abriense" class (cutting, scraping, drilling) and a grinding kit — pebbles with worn edges, slabs, fragments of grinding stones; according to the author, hunting is no longer the main thing, plants were probably already tended (Rodríguez 1989). Level 10 — 7370 ± 130 radiocarbon years (≈ 8400–7950 cal years ago), level 7 — 5600 ± 90. One date of this time.
tepecik-6000: Villages of early farmers in Volcanic Cappadocia (Tepecik-Çiftlik near Niğde). Red-slipped burnished pottery, large vessels with reliefs of people and animals, obsidian of the local volcanoes (Göllüdağ, Nenezi). The settlement lived from ≈ 7100 to ≈ 5800 BC (50 radiocarbon dates; Çakan 2025). Köşk Höyük to the south was founded in the second half of the 7th millennium BC; its early levels are not dated.
central-zagros-6000: Late Neolithic of the valleys of the Central Zagros: Tepe Sarab near Kermanshah, Tepe Guran in the Hulailan valley, villages of the Mahidasht and Harsin plains. Painted pottery with net and "basketry" patterns, later red-slipped ware; goats and sheep, barley. The painted Zagros style lasts from the second half of the 7th into the early 6th millennium BC (Mortensen 1991). Few dates fall on 6000 BC: two dates from Guran are younger than expected for their layers, and the authors doubt them (Marshall 2012).
deh-luran-6000: Deh Luran plain: after Ali Kosh (abandoned by ≈ 6620 BC; Darabi et al. 2024) come the Sefid, Surkh, "transitional Chogha Mami" and Sabz phases (Hole): Chogha Sefid and Tepe Sabz — villages of farmers and herders with painted pottery, irrigation at the end of the sequence. Tepe Sabz: 6925 ± 200 and 6740 ± 190 radiocarbon years — the dates cover the date of the map, with large errors.
susiana-6000: Susiana plain — the Archaic Susiana 0–3 (Chogha Bonut, Chogha Mish, "a village of the 7th millennium"): between the Formative Susiana of Chogha Bonut (until ≈ 6700 BC) and the Early Susiana of Chogha Mish (5716–5542 BC; Alizadeh 2003). Mud-brick houses, painted and burnished pottery related to that of Deh Luran. The plain is on the map by this sequence — there are no direct dates of 6000 BC.
hadramawt-6000: Herders and hunters of southern Arabia in the humid Holocene: thin arrowheads of triangular section ("trihedral"), some of them fluted (a channel flake removed from the base — like the Palaeoindians of America, but independently). In the valleys of Hadramawt — hearths and camps of Manayzah and Khuzmum (Wadi Sana) and HDOR 419 (Wadi Wa'shah): dates of 7270 … 6990 radiocarbon years, about 6000 BC (Crassard 2009; Crassard et al. 2020).
dhofar-6000: Neolithic with trihedral points on the Nejd plateau and the Salalah plain of Dhofar: Hailat Araka — an open stratified site in the far Nejd south of the Rub' al-Khali, trihedral rods in all levels and fluting flakes, 7160 ± 61 radiocarbon years (Zarins 2013); Ad-Dahariz 2 near the Salalah lagoon. Nearby, people with Fasad points may still have lived (Fasad points lasted in Dhofar from ≈ 8000 BC into the 6th millennium BC). In the west, on the border of Mahra — Habarut 1 (excavations of Kh. A. Amirkhanov), its upper layer dated 7400 ± 150 radiocarbon years; further west, to Hadramawt, — about 300 km of Mahra without dated sites.
jebel-faya-6000: Jebel Faya (central Sharjah), FAY-NE10: the third facies of the Neolithic — large tools and trihedral rods, domestic sheep, cremations; a date near 5985 BC at the top of the cremation unit (Uerpmann et al. 2013; Kutterer et al. 2012).
qatar-6000: Camps of hunters and fishers on the Qatar peninsula: hearths with flint tools near Al-Khor on the eastern coast (bifaces, shark bones, shells; Inizan) and under the sand near Shaqah in the south (blade arrowheads of Kapel's "group B"). Two charcoal dates — about 6000 BC, both with large errors: Shaqah K-971 6970 ± 130 (Tauber 1966), Al-Khor MC-2149 6900 ± 200.
jebel-faya-8000: The first Holocene hunters of south-eastern Arabia: blade arrowheads of the Faya (Fasad) type in the FAY-NE1 rockshelter at Jebel Faya and at surface sites of the inner basin of Sharjah; Turbo shells point to links with the coast. Two dates on marine shells — the end of the 9th millennium BC; without a correction for the marine reservoir they are slightly older than the date of the map (Uerpmann et al. 2009, 2013).
khuzestan-6000: Neolithic of the Khuzestan lowlands. On the Deh Luran plain — Chogha Sefid: an unbroken sequence of the Sefid, Surkh, transitional Chogha Mami and Sabz phases (Hole 1977). About 6000 BC this is the late Surkh and the transitional Chogha Mami: houses on stone foundations, platforms of "cigar-shaped" bricks, red Khazineh ware and, next to it, painted ware of Samarran appearance; domestic cattle, the first irrigation canals. A little later, about 5800 BC, comes the Sabz phase: Tepe Sabz and at least five more villages. On the Susiana plain the Archaic Susiana corresponds to the same time (Chogha Bonut, Chogha Mish); then, in both areas, the Early Susiana. Direct dates of 6000 BC are few: the old dates of Chogha Sefid and Tepe Sabz have large errors, and Hole himself rejects some of them.
ayakagytma-6000: Early Kelteminar — hunters, fishers and the first herders of the Kyzylkum desert. The Ayakagytma site above a salt lake in the lower Zeravshan was occupied from c. 6300 to 5400 BC: hearths, flint "horned" trapezes, hand-made pottery; among the bones — wild and possibly domestic cattle, horses and camels.
tutkaul-6000: Hissar culture — mountain hunters and probably the first herders of southern Tajikistan: pebble tools together with microliths, dwellings on slopes. At the Tutkaul settlement on the Vakhsh — burials in a flexed position; by DNA these people are related to ancient Siberians and to the Neolithic population of Iran.
obishir-6000: Obishir culture — hunters and the first herders of the Alai foothills in the south of Fergana (the Obishir 5 and Surungur rockshelters). Microliths, ornaments of stone and bone; by 6000 BC domestic sheep were already kept here — one of the earliest records of herding in Central Asia.
oshkhona-6000: The Oshkhona site in the Markansu valley in the Northern Pamir, at almost 4000 m: tools of Obishir type, bone pendants and beads, bones of sheep or goats. The layers are dated to about 6400–5700 BC.
aq-kupruk-6000: The Aq Kupruk caves in the Balkh gorge (northern Afghanistan). In Ghar-i Mar (Snake Cave) — Neolithic layers with flint sickle inserts and bones of domestic sheep and goats. The dates of the 1960s are about 6400–5100 BC, but some of them do not follow the order of the layers.
loteshwar-6000: Hunter-gatherers on the dunes of North Gujarat: the Loteshwar and Vaarvo Timbo sites, microliths — trapezes, triangles, lunates; hunting of blackbuck and gazelles, gathering of wild grasses. Loteshwar was occupied with breaks from about 7200 to 4700 BC.
bhimbetka-6000: Hunter-gatherers with microliths in the rockshelters of Bhimbetka, famous for their rock paintings, and on the Adamgarh hill by the Narmada; burials right inside the shelters. The dates are old and have large errors — about 7000–5800 BC.
lahuradewa-6000: A settlement by the Lahuradewa lake north of the Ganga: huts on posts, hand-made cord-impressed pottery, rice grains; the earliest dates are of the 7th millennium BC. Whether the rice was already cultivated, and how reliable the early dates are, is still debated.
belan-6000: Early Neolithic at the confluence of the Ganga and the Yamuna (Jhusi) and in the Belan valley (Tokwa, Koldihwa): hand-made cord-impressed pottery, microliths, grinding stones, rice and barley. The excavators place the beginning in the 7th millennium BC, but the dates are old, have large errors and do not follow the order of the layers.
paisra-6000: A site of hunter-gatherers with microliths in the wooded Kharagpur hills south of the Ganga (Bihar). One radiocarbon date — about 6450–6050 BC.
lower-sindh-6000: Hunter-gatherers with microliths at the springs and rivers east of present-day Karachi — on the Mulri Hills and in the Malir and Khadeji valleys; they also gathered mangrove molluscs. Dates exist only for shells from the surface of the sites — about 6600–5500 BC.
yumin-6000: Yumin culture — hunter-gatherers of the south-eastern edge of the Mongolian Plateau (≈ 8800–7000 years ago) who already sowed millet. Semi-subterranean houses, flat-bottomed vessels with net impressions, grinding stones, microblades. Sites — Yumin (Huade) and Xinglong (Kangbao).
tamsagbulag-6000: Tamsagbulag culture — the first known sedentary village in Mongolia (≈ 8400–7300 years ago): rectangular semi-subterranean houses of about 40 m² entered through the roof, burials under the floors, grinding stones, pits with cattle bones.
zaraa-uul-6000: Hunters and gatherers of the Early Neolithic of the Gobi at the foot of the extinct volcano Zaraa Uul, near seasonal lakes: microblades, partly ground adzes, large grinding stones, net-impressed pottery; occupation — 8500–6500 years ago.
hailar-6000: Hunters, fishers and gatherers of the Hulun Buir steppe: large semi-subterranean houses with storage pits, thick shell layers, microblades, flat-bottomed pottery with simple decoration. About 6000 BC — remains of the Huiheshuiba I type (8000–7500 years ago); earlier — Hag I.
song-nen-6000: Fishers and gatherers of the Song-Nen Plain by the lakes of western Jilin: pits, ditches, hand-made pottery with food crusts from cooking freshwater fish; one grain of millet. The dates are on the crusts: because of the fish they may be somewhat older than the true ones.
tolbor-6000: Hunters of the Selenga valley with microblades and one of the oldest potteries in Mongolia: small thin-walled vessels with stamped decoration in rows, also on the rim. Two vessels are dated to about 6500 and about 5650 BC; whether the place was inhabited all that time is unknown.
xiaoshankou-6000: Early farmers and gatherers of northern Anhui (about 6000 BC): flat-bottomed cauldrons, stone axes and adzes, grinding slabs with pestles, objects of bone and antler. Sites — Xiaoshankou and Gutaisi near Suzhou.
shunshanji-6000: Settlements with a ditch on the north-western shore of Lake Hongze (≈ 8500–7500 years ago): round-bottomed cauldrons on clay supports and portable stoves, grinding stones; rice on flooded fields — one of the oldest records of rice farming in the Huai valley.
kaynar-kamar-8000: The Kaynar Kamar rockshelter in the Machay valley (southern Uzbekistan): from the very beginning of the Holocene hunters of mountain goats and sheep returned here again and again — hearths, bladelets and microblades, bone tools; no pottery yet.
houtaomuga-10000: One of the oldest potteries of North-East Asia (≈ 13,000–11,000 years ago): by Lake Xinhuangpao — ditches, pits, coarse hand-made vessels; people caught catfish and gathered freshwater molluscs.
chengbeixi-6000: Chengbeixi culture — the first settled inhabitants of the Yangtze gorges (c. 8500–6900 years ago), an offshoot of the Pengtoushan tradition that came here from the Dongting plain; villages on slopes high above the river, pottery, stone adzes and axes. Sites: Chaotianzui and Sandouping (Zigui, Yichang), Chengbeixi and Zhichengbei (Yidu), the lower layer of Guanmiaoshan (Zhijiang).
niutoushan-6000: Niutoushan on the lower Min River is one of the oldest Neolithic villages of the Fujian coast (c. 8000 years ago): pottery, burnt clay, heaps of freshwater shells; in the authors' view, people came here from the north along the coast, retreating before the rising sea.
qinghai-ne-6000: Hunters with microliths on the north-eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau: in summer — camps on the shores of Qinghai Lake at about 3300 m, in winter — camps with shelters in the Yellow River valley (Shalongka). Wedge-shaped cores and microblades, flint brought from afar; the area was occupied roughly 9000–6200 years ago, then Yangshao farmers arrive. Also the hunting camp of Huangzangsi in the Heihe valley in the Qilian Mountains (c. 8000–6100 years ago).
canxionggashuo-6000: Canxionggashuo on a terrace of the Tongtian River (upper Yangtze, 4030 m) is a large base camp of hunters with microliths (c. 8400–7500 years ago); by the authors' calculations, they did not come down from the plateau even in winter.
osanri-6000: The first settled villages of mainland Korea, on the lagoons of the east coast: pit houses, plain and stamped pottery of the Osan-ri type, pressure-flaked arrowheads, composite fish-hooks, grinding stones; the vessels bear possible impressions of adzuki beans. About 6000–5000 BC; later it is replaced by Yunggimun pottery.
hoabinhian-6000: A technocomplex rather than a single culture: forager groups of caves and river valleys sharing a tradition of pebble tools ("sumatraliths"). The plants they used were wild. The area roughly spans the sites dated close to this time: Con Moong (Vietnam), Tam Hang (Laos), Steep Cliff, Spirit Cave, Lang Kamnan, Moh Khiew (Thailand), Gua Gunung Runtuh (Malaysia), Laang Spean (Cambodia); between them there are no dated sites. In north-eastern Vietnam — the caves of the Bac Son culture (Lang Son, Thai Nguyen, Cao Bang, Bac Kan, Ha Giang, Tuyen Quang): pebble tools with ground edges, later coarse pottery. Vietnamese archaeologists regard it as a separate culture (12,000–5000 years ago), foreign ones as a late variant of the Hoabinhian. When the Hoabinhian ended in the lowlands of northern Vietnam is debated: about 9500 years ago according to foreign syntheses, about 8300–7000 according to Vietnamese ones. On the Shan Plateau (Myanmar) — the Padah-lin caves with ochre paintings. On Sumatra — the shell middens of the north-east coast, Tögi Ndrawa cave on Nias and Gua Pandan in the south of the island.
pawon-6000: Pawon Cave on the shore of the ancient Lake Bandung: burials of flexed bodies coloured with ochre; tools of local obsidian. About 9500–6000 years ago.
toalean-6000: Foragers of the Maros–Pangkep limestone karst: tiny arrowheads with serrated edges (Maros points), backed microliths, bone points; hunting of the Sulawesi warty pig. The Early Toalean — roughly 7500–5500 radiocarbon years ago.
yongjiang-8000: Shell middens on the banks of the Yong River near Nanning: early Holocene foragers (c. 11,000–8500 years ago) ate river molluscs for years, gathered canarium nuts and lotus roots, and buried their dead right in the shell heaps.
mangkalihat: Rockshelters in the Mangkalihat limestone karst: small flakes, freshwater molluscs, turtles; people lived here from the end of the Ice Age, and with the rising sea the coast came closer (about 130 km).
telmana: Mesolithic camps in the Ishim steppes (Northern Kazakhstan): microliths and small blades, seasonal camps by the lakes. At Telmana XIVa charcoal from a pit is dated to about 12,000 years ago (excavations of V. F. Zaibert); the date is single.
aq-kupruk-10000: The Aq Kupruk caves in the foothills of the Hindu Kush (Balkh gorge, northern Afghanistan): blades, flakes, bones of wild goats and sheep. In Ghar-i Asp (Horse Cave) the layer that L. Dupree called "non-ceramic Neolithic" is dated to about 12,000 years ago (one date of the 1960s); later farmers lived in the neighbouring Ghar-i Mar.
aq-kupruk-8000: The Aq Kupruk caves in the Balkh gorge (northern Afghanistan). In Ghar-i Mar (Snake Cave) the "non-ceramic Neolithic" layer of L. Dupree is dated to about 10,000 years ago (one date of the 1960s), between the Upper Palaeolithic below and the pottery Neolithic above. The domestic sheep and goats that Dupree reported for this layer are now doubted.
chikhen-agui: Chikhen Agui — a rockshelter by a spring in the Gobi Altai at about 1970 m: hearths, microblade cores, ostrich-eggshell beads, handles of composite tools. People came here from about 13,400 to 8700 years ago (the Oasis 1 phase of the Gobi, after L. Janz); there are also traces of a visit about 27,000 years ago.
xinglong-10000: Xinglong on the Bashang plateau (Kangbao, northern Hebei): hunters with microblade cores of the North China type, about 13,500–10,000 years ago by the authors; later, about 8700 years ago, pit houses and pottery of the Yumin culture appear at the same place.
tianko-panjang: Tianko Panjang cave in the foothills of the Barisan range (Jambi, Sumatra): thousands of small obsidian flakes from river pebbles, shells and animal bones. Three charcoal dates in the order of the layers — about 12,000–10,000 years ago; pottery appears only in the upper layers, much later.
madai: The caves of the Madai limestone massif in eastern Sabah (Agop Atas, Agop Sarapad): flakes of chert and volcanic rock, pebble hammerstones, bones and shells. About 13,000–7800 years ago (P. Bellwood); then the caves stood empty for thousands of years.
sitai-8000: Sitai on the Bashang plateau (Shangyi, northern Hebei): pit houses, early pottery and microblades already about 10,000 years ago; people returned here again and again (periods about 10,400–10,000 and 9200–9000 years ago, by the authors).
zanskar-8000: Temporary hunters' camps at about 3500–4500 m in Zanskar (Ladakh): hearths and stone tools. About 10,000–9500 years ago (Mune; Pentse-la nearby has a date of the same time); the dates are few.
nejd-leptolithic-8000: Hunters with blade tools (the Nejd Leptolithic) on the Dhofar plateau, from the end of the Pleistocene until c. 7,000 years ago; the dates follow the authors' summary (OSL) and have not been checked site by site. By the dates of Hilbert et al. (2015), the last Leptolithic assemblage (Ghazal GH5) is ≈ 8500 years old; on map 6000* Dhofar already has the Neolithic with trihedral points. In the west — Habarut 1 in Mahra on the border of Oman and Yemen (excavations of Kh. A. Amirkhanov): layers dated about 11,000 and 9500 years ago.
chikoi-10000: Multi-layer settlements on the first terrace of the Chikoi at the mouth of the Menza (Western Transbaikalia): hearths, microblade cores and microblades, scrapers. Early Mesolithic — about 12,700–12,000 years ago (M. V. Konstantinov); lower in the same sections lies one of the earliest pottery of Siberia (about 13,500 years ago).
tytylvaam-8000: A site by Lake Tytyl at the headwaters of the Maly Anyuy (western Chukotka): wedge-shaped microblade cores and microblades, leaf-shaped points, bifaces; a light surface dwelling with a ring of pebbles. About 11,200 and 9600 years ago — the last hunters with Late Palaeolithic techniques in Chukotka.
lower-vitim-8000: Sites near Bodaibo on the lower Vitim (Invalidny III, Pavlova I, Kovrizhka III): microblades from prismatic chert cores, inset knives and scrapers, hearths. About 11,000–9000 years ago, before pottery (A. V. Tetenkin and co-authors).
karasai-8000: A site in the Shilikty valley at the foot of the Saur range (Eastern Kazakhstan): pressure-flaked microblades from prismatic cores, microburins and micro-scrapers. About 10,000 years ago (AMS date on bone) — the first stratified Mesolithic of Eastern Kazakhstan.
haua-fteah-6000: Haua Fteah cave (Cyrenaica): Libyco-Capsian hunter-gatherers (by the model of Douka et al. 2014 — until about 5950 BC) — microliths, gathering of land and sea molluscs. Around 6000–5600 BC goats and sheep appear in the neighbouring Abu Tamsa grotto; pottery at Haua Fteah — from c. 5450 BC.
jefara-6000: Early Neolithic of the Jefara plain at the foot of the Jebel Gharbi (c. 6200–5600 BC, phase A after Barich): seasonal camps by springs and marshes — pottery, bifacial arrowheads, hut floors, ostrich eggshell. No livestock has been found here yet.
mellalian-6000: Ouargla basin: camps by lakes and sebkhas — the Mellalian culture (Hassi Mouillah, El Hadjar, Les Burins; c. 7600–5600 BC): backed bladelets, denticulates, richly decorated ostrich eggshell, ochre. Nearby — the Bordj Mellala I site (c. 6100–5800 BC) with geometric microliths and the first pottery.
el-bayed-6000: El Bayed facies Neolithic (c. 6200–5900 BC): huge camps by ancient sebkhas on the southern edge of the Great Eastern Erg — arrowheads of the Labied and Izimane types, saws, a little pottery, ostrich eggshell. According to G. Camps — at the origins of the Neolithic of the northern Sahara.
zmeilet-6000: Zmeilet el Barka (Saoura valley): a large seasonal hunters' camp on a hill among the dunes, c. 6500–6000 BC; no pottery, engraved ostrich eggshell; by its dates — a contemporary of the early Neolithic sites of El Bayed and El Beida.
atlantic-sahara-6000: Epipalaeolithic hunters of the Atlantic coast of the Sahara — the Foum Arguin culture (north-western Mauritania) and the related Taoukeltian (Tarfaya basin): camps on sandy hills by lakes, tanged spear- and arrowheads, engraved ostrich eggshell; no pottery and no livestock. Time — around the 7th millennium BC (dated by neighbouring finds; c. 5900 BC — eggshell at the Et Teyedché site).
hassi-el-abiod-6000: Hassi el Abiod facies Neolithic (Azawad, northern Mali; c. 6000–3700 BC): kitchen-midden camps by large Holocene lakes — bone harpoons and fish-hooks, Nile perch, turtles, hippopotamus; comb-impressed pottery; burials right in the middens.
oumm-el-assel-6000: Oumm el Assel facies Neolithic (Taoudenni basin, northern Mali; c. 5900–2200 BC): camps of hunters and fishers on the shores of Holocene lakes — bladelets, triangular 'Eiffel Tower' arrowheads, grinding stones, comb-impressed pottery.
acacus-tassili-6000: Tadrart Acacus and Tassili n'Ajjer: rock shelters (Takarkori, Uan Muhuggiag, Ti-n Hanakaten). Around 6000 BC the last hunter-gatherers and fishers (Late Acacus, until c. 6100 BC) give way here to the first herders with sheep, goats and cattle (Early Pastoral, c. 6400–5300 BC); comb-impressed pottery, grinding stones, stone dwellings.
termit-6000: Termit massif (eastern Niger): camps by lakes in the basins of the massif; early pottery — from c. 6000 BC (direct dates on the organic temper of sherds), later — Tenerean.
fachi-6000: Dogonboulo near the Fachi oasis (Ténéré): a camp of fishers and hunters under a layer of lake diatomite, c. 6000 BC — grinding stones, polished axes, pottery, fish bones.
tibesti-6000: Tibesti and the Serir Tibesti: Neolithic sites in the mountains (Gabrong, Ehi Kovmei) and by the lakes of the piedmont plain (Bardagué, c. 6300 BC) — pottery, grinding stones, polished axes; among the bones, next to gazelle, buffalo and giraffe, — sheep and cattle.
sahara-hearths-6000: Hearth sites of nomadic hunters and herders on the plains of the eastern Central Sahara (Wau en Namus, Djebel Eghei): heaps of burnt stones, artefacts, pottery; c. 6200–5800 BC.
hoggar-6000: Hoggar and the Tefedest: the Amekni rockshelter near Tamanrasset, the Tiltekin and Timidouin sites — the 'Neolithic of Saharo-Sudanese tradition': pottery, grinding stones, no farming. Dates — from c. 7700 BC (Amekni) to c. 5700 (Tiltekin) and c. 4950 BC (Timidouin).
sitra-6000: Sitra and El Araq depressions (between Siwa and Bahrein, Western Desert of Egypt): a workshop of blades from the local Sitra chert (c. 6900–6500 BC), then, about 6000–5600 BC, series of stone hearths; there are almost no finds at the hearths, nearby — tools with flat retouch. The northern part is abandoned around 4900 BC.
sodmein-6000: Sodmein Cave and Tree Shelter in the Red Sea Mountains (Egypt): from c. 6200 BC — seasonal camps of herders with goats (the oldest domestic goats of Africa); arrowheads with flat retouch, as in the Western Desert.
laqiya-6000: Laqiya (north-western Sudan): hunters and fishers by the lakes in Wadi Shaw and Wadi Sahal; pottery with the dotted wavy line, later with the criss-cross 'herringbone' (Laqiya type), known only in the Sahara — from Burg et-Tuyur to Wadi Howar.
khartoum-variant-6000: The 'Khartoum Variant' — fishers and hunters of Nubia from the Second Cataract to Sai; pottery with the dotted wavy line. In the Kerma basin about 6000 BC — the initial Neolithic: the El Barga cemetery (6000–5500 BC) with cattle skulls, polished axes and ornaments.
dufuna-6000: A dugout canoe of mahogany (Khaya), 8.4 m long, found 5 m deep in an old channel of the Komadugu Gana near Dufuna (north-eastern Nigeria): one of the oldest boats in the world, c. 6200–6000 BC. No camp was found next to it: the boat belonged to fishers of the river that flowed into Lake Mega-Chad.
pentenga-6000: Péntènga rockshelter at the top of the Gobnangou escarpment (south-eastern Burkina Faso): geometric microliths (crescents, microlithic points, trapezes), fish, freshwater molluscs, aquatic reptiles, oribi and hartebeest; charcoal dates c. 6600–5450 BC. The layers are mixed, so the link between the dates and the microliths is not certain.
bosumpra-6000: Hunter-gatherers of the forest margin of Ghana; the cave was used from the mid-11th millennium BC with breaks. There are no dates around 6000 BC: the nearest ones — c. 7500 and c. 5300 BC — come from one horizon of one trench.
iwo-eleru-6000: Iwo Eleru rockshelter (south-western Nigeria): quartz microliths; about 6000 BC they are joined by bifacial and ground tools of granite and basalt.
dutsen-kongba-6000: Dutsen Kongba rockshelter on the Jos Plateau (Nigeria): quartz microliths (microlithic points, crescents, trapezes, scrapers), rare unpolished bifaces, pottery with comb and stick impressions. The oldest date is c. 6050–5500 BC, the site was used until c. 3400 BC; the start of occupation rests on a single old date.
shum-laka-6000: Shum Laka rockshelter (Grassfields, Cameroon): hunter-gatherers with quartz microliths; about 6000 BC — the first burials, the first pottery, bifaces and ground tools (the start of the 'Stone to Metal Age', after Lavachery).
tshitolian-6000: The Tshitolian industry: hunter-gatherers of the forest-savanna mosaic with small bifaces and arrowheads. Ntadi Yomba (Niari valley) — a hearth of c. 6000 BC, bones of rhinoceros and duikers; in southern Gabon (Ndendé) — the final phase; it lasted until the arrival of farmers in the 1st millennium BC.
lope-6000: Lopé 2 in the middle Ogooué valley (Gabon), a savanna patch within the forest: quartz flakes and bladelets dated c. 6650–6400 and c. 5900–5500 BC. Older layers (13,000–12,000 years ago) have Tshitolian-like tools, but this horizon is not attributed to the Tshitolian.
abhe-6000: The northern shore of ancient Lake Abhe (lower Awash, Afar, Ethiopia): settlements c. 6250–5450 BC — before, during and after the dry event of 8,200 years ago. Obsidian bladelets, curved backed pieces (tips of arrows or harpoons), grinding stones; catfish, tilapia, hippopotamus, crocodile. No pottery and no livestock: herders came only c. 2850 BC.
simbero-6000: Simbero rockshelter at 3519 m in the Bale Mountains (Ethiopia): a mid-Holocene phase from c. 6150 BC — dense microliths (segments, crescents), scrapers, borers, bones of wild animals; people stayed for long periods. Within the phase there are no dates between c. 6150 and c. 3350 BC.
buri-6000: Shell middens of the Buri Peninsula and the Gulf of Zula (Eritrea): Gelalo NW and Misse East — obsidian bladelets and backed pieces, beads of shell and ostrich eggshell, mangrove and lagoon shells; c. 6500–5500 BC. The dates are on marine shells (with a reservoir correction), the excavations are small.
turkana-6000: Fishers and hunters on the shores of Lake Turkana, then larger than today: barbed bone harpoons, decorated pottery (Lothagam, Lowasera, Napudet). Dates close to 6000 BC are on shell and fish bone; a hearth charcoal at Napudet is c. 5450–4850 BC. Many sites have several phases separated by centuries or millennia; fishing lasted until the end of the wet period c. 3000 BC.
kansyore-6000: Early Kansyore: fishers, hunters and gatherers on the north-eastern shores of Lake Victoria, with some of the earliest pottery of eastern Africa. Namaboni B (Busia, Uganda) — a shell midden with quartz tools, fish bones and burials, c. 7000–5000 BC; Pondo (north Nyanza, Kenya) — c. 6000–5500 BC.
lukenya-6000: Rockshelter GvJm-19 on Lukenya Hill (Athi–Kapiti plains, Kenya): Later Stone Age tools of chert and quartz, bones of wild savanna ungulates; the Holocene deposit is one unit c. 7000–2650 BC, with pottery in its upper part. All dates are on bone apatite, which tends to give too young ages.
nachikufan-6000: Nachikufan IIA at Mwela Rocks (granite hills east of Kasama, northern Zambia): mostly backed flakes rather than bladelets, the first ground stone axe, bored stones and grinding stones. Phase IIA lasts c. 9200–5700 BC; the date close to 6000 BC is a single sample of the 1960s (± 200 years).
nachikufan-8000: Nachikufan IIA at Mwela Rocks (granite hills east of Kasama, northern Zambia): mostly backed flakes rather than bladelets, the first ground stone axe, bored stones and grinding stones. The date for this map — c. 8300–7100 BC — is a single date of the 1960s; the phase continues at Mwela until c. 6000 BC.
apollo11-6000: Apollo 11 Cave in the Huns Mountains (southern Namibia), layer C: a mostly microlithic set — convex scrapers, segments, backed tools, beads and engraved pieces of ostrich eggshell, pendants of marine shell; charcoal dates c. 6350–5900 BC, the layer spans c. 8650–5150 BC. In the neighbouring Pockenbank cave there is a single hearth of about the same time.
mirabib-6000: Mirabib rockshelter by the Kuiseb valley (central Namib, Namibia): the densest occupation is in layers F–D — thousands of stone tools of typical Wilton type (segments, bladelets, thumbnail scrapers; 92–95 % of rock crystal), about 3 kg of ostrich eggshell, bones, seeds of the !nara melon. Dates c. 7450–6850 and c. 5600–5200 BC.
tsodilo-6000: Depression rockshelter in the Tsodilo Hills (north-western Botswana): a charcoal date of c. 6050–5750 BC together with the deepest mongongo nut shells (food). The date is single and there are few finds in the layer; in the neighbouring White Paintings shelter, fishers with harpoons appear later, c. 5,700–4,100 years ago.
apollo11-8000: Apollo 11 Cave and the Rosh Pinah rockshelter (southern Namibia, near the Orange River): early Holocene hunter-gatherers with microliths; dates c. 9100–8100 BC.
izriten-10000: The Izriten dune by the Khnifiss lagoon (Tarfaya coast, southern Morocco): hunter-gatherers without pottery, burials of people of Mechtoid type; dates c. 10,300 and c. 8800 BC.
nachikufan-i-10000: Nachikufan I — hunter-gatherers of northern Zambia with tiny backed bladelets, scrapers, bored stones and grinding stones; at the Mwela Rocks rockshelter — c. 13,400–11,500 cal BP (a date with a large error). Similar tools are found in the Lunsemfwa basin (Mwambachimo, until c. 9000 BP).
bosumpra-5000: Hunter-gatherers of the forest margin of Ghana; the cave was used from the mid-11th millennium BC with breaks. The date nearest to 5000 BC is c. 5300 BC (horizon 2 of one trench); the author places horizons 2 and 5 between the 11th and the end of the 5th millennium BC (Watson 2017).
britain-5000: Late Mesolithic of Britain: narrow geometric microliths (from c. 8,400 years ago); it lasts until the Neolithic arrives about 4000 BC. Britain is already an island. Sites dated to about 6000 BC — from Cornwall and Gower to Scotland: Howick, Morton, Balneaves, Bolsay (Islay), West Runton, Inverness, An Corran (Skye), Ulva. In western Scotland — the "Obanian" shell middens (Druimvargie near Oban, Oronsay): most authors see them as camps of the same people for processing shellfish and fish, not as a separate culture.
central-france-5000: The "second" Mesolithic with trapezes in western and central France: from the Loire and Burgundy south to Auvergne, Cantal, Velay, Rouergue and Quercy, west to the Charente and the mouth of the Gironde; it lasts until about the arrival of the Neolithic (c. 5000–4800 BC). No regional groups are defined yet. Sites dated to about 6000 BC — Cuze de Neussargues and Les Baraquettes (Cantal), Béraud and Longetraye (Velay), Roquemissou (Aveyron), Lascaux, Pergourie, Geay, Lède du Gurp, Bavans rockshelter (Doubs).
lower-amur-5000: Fishers and hunters of the Lower Amur with flat-based pottery and prismatic cores. Around 6000 BC, settlements are dated here at Suchu (near Mariinskoe), Malaya Gavan and in the lower layer of Sakachi-Alyan. I. Ya. Shevkomud assigns them to the early stage of the Kondon culture, V. E. Medvedev to the Mariinsky and early Malyshevo cultures. By recent dates the Kondon culture lasts until about 4500 BC, followed by the Malyshevo culture.
new-ireland-5000: Ancestors of the Papuans. The island was never joined to New Guinea. Matenbek cave (dates down to c. 6,700 years ago) and Buang Merabak on the east coast, Balof 2 in the north (dates down to c. 7,000 years ago): hunting of the cuscus, gathering of shellfish; obsidian was brought from New Britain. Panakiwuk cave was abandoned already c. 8,000 radiocarbon years ago.
nostvet-lihult-5000: Nøstvet–Lihult: the Late Mesolithic of south-eastern Norway and western Sweden — the Skagerrak coast from Lista to Göteborg, the lowland around the Oslofjord and the shores of Lake Vänern with Värmland. Nøstvet begins c. 6300 BC (ground axes, microliths), the Lihult culture of western Sweden c. 5900 BC; both last until about 4600–4400 BC. Sites dated to about 6000 BC — Skoklefall, Kvestad, Krøgenes, Ullern (Norway), Gunnarsröd, Ödsmål, Kvernos, Vestanvik (Sweden); to about 5000 BC — Solli (Norway).
oaxaca-5000: Hunters and gatherers of the Valley of Oaxaca: Guilá Naquitz and Cueva Blanca caves and the open camp of Gheo-Shih by the Mitla River (lower layer about 7600 BC). In Marcus and Flannery's scheme the Naquitz phase gives way about 6000 BC to the Jícaras phase, which lasts until about 4000 BC.
paleo-arctic-5000: Late Denali complex — hunters with microblades and wedge-shaped cores (American Paleo-Arctic tradition) in interior Alaska, the Brooks Range, the upper Susitna and south-west Yukon. Sites dated to about 6000 BC: Onion Portage, Dry Creek, Broken Mammoth, Panguingue Creek, Owl Ridge, Teklanika West; in the Brooks Range — Tingmiukpuk and Gallagher; on the upper Susitna — Jay Creek Ridge. In south-west Yukon (Canyon, Annie Lake) — the Little Arm phase with microblades (c. 8,000 to 4,500 years ago). From about 6000 radiocarbon years ago (c. 4850 BC) Alaska has the Northern Archaic with side-notched points.
puna-jujuy-5000: Vicuña and guanaco hunters of the middle puna (Middle Archaic). About 6000 and 5000 BC — Hornillos 2 (layer 3; Susques); the earlier sites of the zone — Huachichocana, Inca Cueva, Pintoscayoc — are abandoned or in a gap by about 6000 BC.
southern-new-england-5000: Middle Archaic of southern New England: Neville and Stark points, quartz tools; it lasts until about 4000 BC. The Neville type site lies at Amoskeag Falls on the Merrimack (New Hampshire). Sites dated to about 6000 BC: Annasnappet Pond, Seekonk 2 (Massachusetts); Sandy Hill (Connecticut) — the latest date about 8000 years ago.
wilton-5000: Hunter-gatherers of southern Africa with the microlithic Wilton industry (segments, small scrapers, ostrich eggshell beads; c. 8,000–4,000 years ago): Melkhoutboom, Matjes River, Nelson Bay, Wonderwerk, Rose Cottage. The non-microlithic Oakhurst with large 'Woodlot' scrapers in the Lesotho highlands and in the north (Sehonghong, Liphofung, Kruger Cave) lives on until about 5600 BC. The dry interior — the Karoo and Namaqualand — was thinly settled about 6000 BC.
jeitun-5000: Jeitun culture — the first farmers of Central Asia (c. 6300–4800 BC). About 6000 BC — two clusters of villages at the foot of the Kopet Dag: around Jeitun and Geok Tepe (Chopan, Togolok) and in the south-east, near Meana and Chaacha (Monjukli Depe, Chagylly); further west, as far as Bami, Jeitun villages appear later. Late Jeitun (c. 5200–4800 BC) — Chakmakly, Chagylly II, Monjukli II; then Anau IA. One-room houses of clay blocks with a hearth, barley and wheat, goats and sheep.
el-prodigio-5000: El Prodigio (El Limón, Chaparral, southern Tolima): an open-air site on a ridge of the eastern slope of the Central Cordillera (800–1000+ m) with a dark anthropogenic soil. Small flakes of chert and quartz of the "Abriense" class (cutting, scraping, drilling) and a grinding kit — pebbles with worn edges, slabs, fragments of grinding stones; according to the author, hunting is no longer the main thing, plants were probably already tended (Rodríguez 1989). Level 10 — 7370 ± 130 radiocarbon years (≈ 8400–7950 cal years ago), level 7 — 5600 ± 90; there are no dates in between.
hadramawt-5000: Herders and hunters of southern Arabia in the humid Holocene: thin arrowheads of triangular section ("trihedral"), some of them fluted (a channel flake removed from the base — like the Palaeoindians of America, but independently). In the valleys of Hadramawt — hearths and camps of Manayzah and Khuzmum (Wadi Sana) and HDOR 419 (Wadi Wa'shah): dates of 7270 … 6990 radiocarbon years, about 6000 BC (Crassard 2009; Crassard et al. 2020). About 5000 BC the next phase is already here: the Arabian Bifacial Tradition (Sueyhian facies; HDOR 410).
jefara-5000: Early Neolithic of the Jefara plain at the foot of the Jebel Gharbi (phase A after Barich; the sites were occupied c. 8100–5600 cal years ago, c. 6150–3650 BC): seasonal camps by springs and marshes — pottery, bifacial arrowheads, hut floors, ostrich eggshell. No livestock has been found here yet.
dniester-bug-5000: The Dniester and Southern Bug: the Bug–Dniester culture (Soroca, Sokol'tsy II, Pechera) — hunters and fishers who adopt pottery at the beginning of the 6th millennium BC; its late sites reach the end of the 6th — beginning of the 5th millennium BC. Its predecessor is the Mesolithic Grebeniki culture (Budjak, the lower Dniester — Mirnoe, Grebeniki), until about 6000 BC.
balangoda-5000: Balangoda culture of Sri Lanka: rainforest hunter-gatherers with microliths, known from c. 38,000 to c. 3,000 years ago (Fa-Hien-lena cave, Bellan-bandi Palassa, Kuragala). The zone also includes the south coast at the Bundala lagoons (Patirajawela, by OSL ≈ 7.6 thousand years ago).
eastern-sahara-5000: Hunter-gatherers and herders of the Western (Libyan) Desert: Nabta — Kiseiba, Dakhla, Kharga, Farafra (Wadi el-Obeiyid), Abu Minqar, Selima, the Gilf Kebir. A common 'bifacial' tradition: arrowheads with flat retouch, grinding stones, round huts on stone slabs; pottery in the 'Khartoum' style — from the mid-7th millennium BC; goats and sheep — from c. 6000 BC. About 5000 BC — the Late Neolithic of Nabta, Bashendi B in Dakhla, Kharga C; the Djara plateau and Regenfeld are abandoned by then.
latnija-6000: Hunter-gatherers of Latnija cave (Mellieħa, northern Malta): stone tools, hearths, food remains. Occupation from about 6500 to 5500 BC (c. 8,500–7,500 years ago; Scerri et al. 2025): people reached the island by sea. The first farmers (Għar Dalam) reach Malta about 5900 BC.
uninhabited-balearics: Balearic Islands: people arrive here only about 2300 BC.
uninhabited-ice-5000: The last remnants of the Laurentide ice sheet: the Labrador dome over northern Quebec (Nunavik) with a small piece near Lake Michikamau, and the ice on the Melville Peninsula (after the reconstruction of Dyke et al. 2003, slice c. 6,850 years ago). The ice on Southampton and Baffin Islands lies within the zone “Uninhabited — Canadian Arctic Archipelago”. The ice sheet was gone completely about 6,700 years ago (Ullman et al. 2016).
central-chile-5000: Middle Archaic of central Chile (Archaic III of Cornejo and Saavedra, ≈ 8100–5600 cal years ago): hunter-gatherers of the foothills and valleys from the Aconcagua to the former Tagua Tagua lagoon (Cuchipuy cemetery) and of the coast at Bucalemu (Paso de las Conchas shell midden, until 3780 BC). In the south, at Curicó, — the Tutuquén cemetery: the second Archaic occupation, ≈ 18 burials, c. 5300–4700 BC; Loanco A points and grinding stones. Seasonal camps in the valleys and on the coast, short stays in mountain rockshelters (Los Piuquenes, El Manzano).
taltal-5000: Fishers and gatherers of the Taltal coast — the "shell fish-hook culture" (Archaic III, ≈ 7500–5500 cal years ago; Salazar et al. 2015): 11 camps along ≈ 70 km of coast from Los Bronces to Zapatero, dense shell middens, semi-subterranean houses at Morro Colorado, circular fish-hooks of Choromytilus mussel shell, fishing for jack mackerel; almost no burials. Zapatero — 6180 ± 25 radiocarbon years (≈ 7040 cal years ago). The authors do not include Taltal in the Chinchorro tradition.
copaca-5000: Copaca 1 — a large shell midden 30 km south of Tocopilla (up to 2.5 m of deposits, at least nine occupation episodes): a semi-sedentary camp of fishers and gatherers — jack mackerel and other fish, shellfish, sea lions, burials with ochre, a stone structure. It begins c. 5900 BC and continues c. 4500–3100 BC (Castro et al. 2016); there are no dates right around 5000 BC.
upper-loa-6000: Middle Archaic camelid hunters of the upper Loa (northern Chile, ≈ 3000 m): the Chulqui rockshelter near Toconce — 7180 ± 80 radiocarbon years (c. 6200–5850 BC); nearby — the Huiculunche rockshelter (Turi wetland). Pentagonal and lanceolate points; in the dry middle Holocene people kept to a few places with water (De Souza 2004).
upper-loa-5000: Middle Archaic camelid hunters of the upper Loa (northern Chile, ≈ 3000 m): the Huiculunche (Turi wetland) and Punta Brava (Loa canyon at Santa Bárbara) rockshelters — pentagonal and lanceolate points, stone brought from the high puna. Huiculunche — 6120 ± 40 radiocarbon years (c. 5200–4850 BC), Punta Brava — 6250 ± 240. In the dry middle Holocene people kept to a few places with water (De Souza 2004).
plateau-des-mines-5000: The earliest traces of people in French Guiana — the Archaic (≈ 6000 radiocarbon years ago): the Plateau des Mines site (Carrière des Ananas) near Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, on the white sands of the coastal plain — heaps of quartz pebbles, earth ovens, no pottery; four charcoal dates, c. 5300–4900 BC. The Eva 2 site near Kourou is younger (c. 4400–3900 BC).
cubilan-5000: The Cubilán area near Oña (southern highlands of Ecuador, 2400–3190 m): workshops for quarrying and first working of local chert; starch grains on the tools point to maize and wild yam (some identifications are preliminary). The last camps of stage II — the Loma Blanca rockshelter and Cu-S4, c. 4900 BC (6070 ± 25 radiocarbon years), then a gap of more than 1300 years (Pagán-Jiménez et al. 2021).
middle-cauca-5000: Preceramic foragers of the Cauca basin: the Middle Cauca (Caldas, Risaralda, Quindío), El Jazmín to the north in Antioquia, and the Calima preceramic tradition to the south-west. On the slope of the Western Cordillera near the town of Andes — La Querida: stone tools with grinding and flaking, part of the stone brought from afar; 6190 ± 70 and 5870 ± 100 radiocarbon years (c. 5300–4500 BC); 12 potsherds were found too — whether this is early pottery or the sherds came down from above, the authors leave open (Agudelo et al. 1999). Hoe-axes with notches for hafting, grinding stones, no projectile points; plant gathering, small game hunting, fishing.
penones-5000: The Peñones de Bogotá terrace on the west bank of the Magdalena at Puerto Berrío (Antioquia; a local name, unrelated to Bogotá): unifacial and bifacial tools of chert, quartzite and quartz — point fragments, scrapers, choppers, flat pebbles for grinding plants. Charcoal from the layer with the tools — 5980 ± 90 radiocarbon years (c. 5200–4600 BC). According to the authors, late preceramic groups of the Middle Magdalena, continuing a bifacial tradition thousands of years old (López, Botero 1993).
las-vegas-5000: Late Las Vegas — fishers, hunters and gatherers of the Santa Elena Peninsula, Ecuador. It was long thought that after c. 5300 BC the peninsula was empty until Valdivia; but squash phytoliths at sites 67 and 80 and maize pollen in the Punta Carnero core (c. 4900–4500 BC), as well as the preceramic layers of Real Alto and Loma Atahualpa, show that people stayed (Stahl, Stothert 2020; Popov, Tabarev 2023).
las-mercedes-5000: Two sites 2 km apart in the Andean foothills north-east of Santo Domingo (upper Esmeraldas basin, ≈ 750 m): a buried soil under many layers of volcanic ash, with stone tools of early hunter-gatherers; two occupation episodes, ten charcoal dates — c. 5500–4300 BC (Constantine 2017). Pottery appears here only c. 1100 BC (Chorrera).
porce-6000: Preceramic hunter-gatherers of the middle Porce (Antioquia, 800–1000 m; the Porce II reservoir area): the lower layers with burials on the terraces — 7040 ± 60 and 7080 ± 130 radiocarbon years (c. 6000–5800 BC); stone tools, grinding stones; the occupation continues without a break until c. 4400 BC (Castillo, Aceituno 2000).
porce-5000: Preceramic hunter-gatherers of the middle Porce (Antioquia, 800–1000 m; the Porce II reservoir area): an artificial earth mound with burials on a terrace (Y-021), stone tools, grinding stones. According to the authors, a continuous occupation c. 5900–4400 BC (7040 ± 60 … 5670 ± 70 radiocarbon years), then the first potters of La Cancana (Castillo, Aceituno 2000).
puna-junin-5000: Vicuña and guanaco hunters of the Junín and Huánuco puna; the Lauricocha II phase (according to Salcedo — c. 5900–2800 BC): triangular points, in the puna the domestication of llamas and alpacas begins. On the date — Telarmachay (layer Vc), Panaulauca (phase 3), Pachamachay.
ayacucho-5000: Hunters and gatherers of the Ayacucho Basin (MacNeish excavations). The upper layers of the Puente rockshelter — the Piki phase: 6030 ± 120 radiocarbon years (c. 5200–4550 BC); then the Chihua phase (Rosamachay, c. 4500–4000 BC). The dates are old, with large errors.
mongoncillo-5000: A preceramic coastal industry of the Casma and Huarmey coast: bipolar (anvil) knapping, awls, scrapers, denticulates; 38 sites on the hills (lomas) by the sea at Casma and the large site PV35-106 near Huarmey. According to Bonavia — local descendants of the Paiján people who turned to fishing and gathering and lived almost sedentarily by the shore. The dating is disputed: according to Salcedo — 5100–4600 BC (El Calvario, Cerro Negro); according to Bonavia and Uceda, these dates belong to the final preceramic and Mongoncillo is a few centuries older; PV35-106 — 6430 ± 175 radiocarbon years (c. 5650–4950 BC).
south-central-andes-5000: Middle Archaic foragers in the highlands of Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna, in the south-west of the Titicaca basin and in the Arica precordillera and highlands. Near the date of the map — Asana (Moquegua; 6040 ± 90 radiocarbon years, c. 5200–4700 BC), Sumbay (Arequipa) and Jaquenasa cave (4100 m, upper Lauca; 6200 ± 80, c. 5300–4850 BC). Asana was occupied with breaks from the Early Archaic until ≈ 3500 radiocarbon years ago.
pozo-cavado-5000: Abrigo Pozo Cavado — a rockshelter on the edge of the Salar de Pocitos (western puna of Salta, ≈ 3700 m): bones of vicuña and guanaco, lanceolate bifacial points, blade technique. Occupations c. 6400–5000 and c. 4700–3900 BC and later; near the date of the map — 6280 ± 90 radiocarbon years on bone (Orsi, López 2019).
